The House in Committee on Private Bills, Air. Rhodes in the Chair.
Bill No. 19, respecting a patent of James W. Owen-Air. Aliddlebro-in Committee.
This is the Bill that was up the other night, when there was nobody present to explain it. Is there any one here now to explain it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman who introduced this Bill is not present. I understand he went home on Friday night and has been detained in consequence of the train service being disorganized. I have looked at the papers in the Department of Agriculture, which has jurisdiction over patents, and am prepared to explain the Bill ito the committee.
In this case an inventor named Owen obtained a patent in the United States for a device in connection with a sound reproducing machine, on the 9th December, 1915. He also, about the same time, obtained patents in several other foreign countries for this invention. The Canada Patent Act, section 8, requires that an inventor who has obtained a patent in a foreign country should make his application in Canada for a patent within one year of the time at which he has obtained this foreign patent. This was not done, and he asks an extension of time. He presented reasons for this request which were satisfactory to the committee and they reported in favour of the Bill. The facts are that, well within the prescribed time, Air. Owen gave the necessary instructions to a prominent firm of patent attorneys in the United States to make application in Canada for a patent, but that owing to the long illness, resulting in the death, of the patent attorney in whose hands this business had been placed, the matter was overlooked

I was not at the meeting of the Private Bills Committee when this Bill went through and therefore I suppose I ought not to come here and find fault. But, it seems to me that we might as well repeal our whole Patent Act as to allow Bills of this kind to be continually put through Parliament. It does not seem to make any difference how negligent a man may have been with reference to carrying

out the provisions of the Patent Act; if he has money enough to pay his fee, and retain some solicitor to make a reasonable excuse, he can get his patent through. This has been going on ever since I have been in Parliament, and I must say that the nuisance is getting worse every year; in fact, I think there have been more of these Bills going through Parliament in the last three years than during all the time since I first came to Parliament. You have heard the explanation which the hon. the acting Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hazen) gives this afternoon, and he gives it, of course, in perfectly good faith. A man hands over such an important thing as the obtaining of a patent for something which he looks upon as being valuable and he says that he places it in the hands of a solicitor who becomes ill.	Is there any man in this
House innocent enough to believe that that man did not know that this solicitor was ill, that a man who takes the trouble to obtain a patent in a foreign country is not looking after his interests sufficiently to know that his solicitor is ill? I do not believe it at all. That may be a very strong statement to make, but I have seen too many of these excuses put before this House during the last ten or eleven years and I am beginning to look with suspicion on every one of them. I will vote against the passage of this Bill. I do not know who the parties are and I do not know what the value of the patent may be. It may be worth $10,000,000, or $100,000 or it may not be worth $1. I think the time has come when we should stop that sort of business. We have enough provisions in the Patent Act by which any reasonable omission can be corrected by the patent office itself. I had a case not long ago where an American manufacturer honestly came to Canada in order to try to obtain a factory in which to manufacture his invention, but on account of the factories being so taken up with the manufacture of munitions of war he was unable to -carry out his purpose. He made an affidavit setting forth the facts and he put it before the patent office. They held that this affidavit was sufficient and they gave him an extension of time for one year within which to commence the manufacture of the patented article in Canada. But this man has entirely slept upon his rights; he has not applied to the patent office in Canada within one year of the time at which he obtained his patent in a foreign country. To show the fallacy of granting this extension: there are a

number of other reasons for which a patent may become void, and one of the principal ones is that if the article has been on sale in any foreign country for a longer term than one year prior to making the application in Canada, the applicant cannot get his patent here. We have no evidence that this article may not have been on sale two or three years in the United States before the application was made in Canada, and if that is so the patent never should be granted. Yet, by this Bill, the man is reinstated with all his rights, no matter how much he may have violated the provisions of the Canadian law before that, the only palliation being that there is something like a year taken off the life of his patent at the other end eighteen years hence. I do not think any patentee will feel that he is called upon to make any very great sacrifice by tire fact that his patent shall be for seventeen years instead of eighteen years. I make these observations without any feeling in the matter I am registering this protest on principle, and I hope the time will come when this Parliament will 'Stop reinstating men in patent rights when (they have either violated, or neglected to observe, practically every provision of the patent law of Canada.

Will the minister
tell the committee whether the person asking for this exceptional treatment is a Canadian or belongs to some other country?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He belongs to the town ol Lansdowne, Pennsylvania. That is set out in the preamble of the Bill. I may say, in regard to what has been said by my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Car veil) that I do not know who this gentleman is, nor do I know anything about him, but it would appear that he has acted in good faith in regard to the matter. That, of course, was a matter for the Private Bills Committee to ascertain and he satisfied the committee by affidavits that are produced here and which show his bona fides. It seems to me that under circumstances of this sort, when a man swears that he, still within twelve months of the time when he obtained his patent in the United -States, placed his business in the hands of a reputable patent attorney with instructions to make his application in Canada, that the attorney became ill, that the matter was neglected and that, in consequence of that fact, he did not make his application, there is reason which would justify this Parliament in granting this extension. The case presented is one that seems to have justified the Private Bills Committe in coming to a conclusion to recommend it. Apparently there could be no reason why he should delay his application for twelve months after he obtained his patent in the United States. If he actually did not, and if he gave instructions to a reputable attorney to have this patent taken out in Canada and if, through the illness of that attorney, and through no fault of the applicant, that was not done, there seems to me to be a fair case made out why this Parliament should exercise its right and grant him the right to take out a patent under the patent law of the land for the length of time which the patent would have run if taken out in the first instance within the time provided by law.

Notwithstanding the explanation made by the minister, I would like to see this Bill go back to the Private Bills Committee. I would like to see the ' Private Bills Committee bring this man before them. It is a simple matter to draw an affidavit which means nothing and yet is not perjury. He says that he put this matter into the hands of a solicitor who has since died. That may be all true and yet there may be no excuse in it. I would like to know if the attorney had a partner, a well-organized office, a number of clerks in his office, or somebody else, to carry on his business, and I would like to know whether all the business in that solicitor's hands was allowed to lapse for months because the solicitor was ill and subsequently died. I venture to say there Is not a word of that kind of explanation in the affidavit and yet I dare say that every word in the affidavit may be true, but even if the condition that I have suggested is true it is no excuse why this Parliament should step in and rectify these blunders and omissions. A patent is an important thing. A mSn who invents a new or useful article is entitled by law to protection in the manufacture and sale of that article so long as he complies with the laws of that country. If he does not comply with the laws of the country he is not entitled to protection -and the people of this country generally are entitled to the use of that article. Every day we are deliberately thrusting away from, our own people the right to the use of something which some foreigner has invented and has failed by his negligence to protect himself in the use of in Canada; and yet, we are stepping in and

giving him these valuable rights. I would like to see this Bill go back to the Private Bills Committee and I would like to see the Private Bills Committee establish the precedent of bringing these gentlemen before the committee and having them sworn so that we would have a chance of examining and cross-examining them in order to see if the real reason has been given for the negligence in this and other cases.

The situation in regard to this Bill would vary somewhat depending on whether the applicant for exceptional treatment was a citizen of Canada or whether he came from some other country. After all, what is done under the Patent Act is to give certain persons, by way of a premium upon invention, the exclusive right to manufacture and sell the particular articles which they have produced. The inventor is given that privilege at the expense of the public in Canada who must pay tribute to him either by royalty or in some other way is they desire to use the article. In regard to the question of amendments to the patent law, I have deemed it my duty on various occasions to note with some care the measures which have been submitted to this Parliament giving special rights to parties who made lapses and departures from the statute. In most cases, although various reasons were put forward by the parties, it would seem that, as a matter of fact, the party had discovered that the article which he had produced had proved to be of some greater value than he had at first suggested and that the neglect to comply with the statute was due to a cause of that kind more than to any reason such as could be forward in this particular case. What is the proposition before the committee? That this man living in Lansdowne, Pa., who has an article which he has patented in the United States, and which could not be patented in Canada under the procedure more than a year after the date of having obtained the patent there, has forfeited his right of imposing on the Canadian people the exclusive right of manufacture and sale which would otherwise be his under the Patent Act. It is all very well for a solicitor to present a Bill to this House and give as a reason that his attorney was ill and that therefore the matter was neglected. I see no reason whatever why Parliament should go outside of the Patent Act and give any special rights to this gentleman who happens to belong to another country. This is very exceptional treatment and if the law as it has been laid down, and has not been amended, is to be disregarded,
I Mr. Carvell.'J
do not let us disregard it for people outside of Canada who are to be given special privileges. By what reason are we to say that manufacturers in Canada could not go on and produce the article which this gentleman could have patented freely and without any restriction? Why should we impose a tax, by way of royalty, on anybody in Canada who wanted to produce it for the benefit of this gentleman in the United States who did not choose to have his business looked after? The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) says that this gentleman engaged an attorney in the United States, and that the attorney fell ill and, did not attend to the business. I submit, as a professional man, that it would be very curious indeed if that occurred. Was there only one lawyer in that firm; was there no other lawyer looking after the business of this attorney? What was happening to all his other interests while he was prevented from attending to such an ordinary matter as looking after this patent? Even supposing that the claim submitted is true, and I suppose we must presume, prima facie, that it is true, that is not sufficient for this Parliament to go out of its road to give to an alien such advantage over the Canadian people.

Did the Government take up with the British Government the question of greater co-operation in immigration, in accordance with an offer contained in a letter from the Right Honourable John Burns, President of the Local Government Board to Mr. Arthur Hawkes, published by authority of the Hon. Robert Rogers in a special report on immigration, in May, 1912? If so, what progress has been made?

The immigration efforts of ihe Dominion Government are confined to securing for Canada agriculturists, and, at times, female domestic servants. That, in the opinion of this House, the organization of a Department of Public Health is desirable in order to conserve in the largest measure possible the physical welfare of the people of this Dominion.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this question has been considered in a more or less casual manner by the different Governments of Canada for the past thirty years; hut at no time in the past has the subject been so urgent as it is to-day.
It is amazing at this period of the world's history to read in even a few of our Canadian papers editorials which display a lamentable ignorance of the present day [DOT]significance of the (term public health. Whenever the subject is referred to, these journals, with gross ignorance of the subject and possibly with some prejudice, interpret it as having reference only to one phase of the medical profession. This view of public health might have been excusable half a century ago, but any person who looks at it in that light to-day merely illustrates the fact, all too apparent, that the subject has not received that intelligent consideration by those assuming to educate our people that its vast importance demands.
At the outset let me say a word to disabuse the minds of a few suspicious and' misinformed people and newspapers who are labouring under a misapprehension regarding the object aimed at by this resolution. Permit me to say, it has no reference whatever to the subject of medical education nor to the teachings or' beliefs of any school of medicine.
I said that this subject has been discussed in Parliament before; but, in view of the great development which Canada will experience in the near future, and in view of the wonderful advance that has been anede in the science of public health even in the last ten years, no apology is required on my part for its re-introduction at this time. The fact that the Dominion of Canada almost alone among the-larger nations of the world has no department of public health, so defined, rests upon the basis upon which the Confederation of Canada was formed as set forth in the British North America Act. In 1867 little thought was given ,to public health problems, and the British North. America Act makes . no reference whatever to public health as a function of government. The Act merely states that census and statistics are under the Federal Government, while the management of hospitals, asylums and charities is left under the charge of provincial Government. There has always

been some confusion in the minds of our Canadian people regarding the authority of the Federal Government to deal with health matters.
The British North America Act, section 91, declares that the exclusive legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects enumerated, and among other subjects mentions (1) census and statistics and (2) quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals. Under section 92, enumerating exclusive powers of provincial legislatives, are named among others:
The establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums and charities and [DOT] eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other1 than marine hospitals.
Practically all health work done dn 1867 fell under " Quarantine and Marine Hospitals." Section 91 further states that:
It shall be lawful for the Federal Government of Canada to legislate on all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the- Legislatures of the Provinces.
This appears with absolute clearness to give power to this Parliament to deal with public health matters, for the only phases of public health assigned to the provinces by the British North America Act are the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums and charities. In so far then as the Federal Government in the interest , of the State desires to perform public health work, it has competent power under the constitution to do so.
At the time of Confederation little thought was given to public health problems. No state in the American Union nor any province of Canada had a health department. It is not surprising therefore that a subject of so little interest at that time" should receive such scant mention when the powers of the various legislatures were being defined by the Fathers of Confederation. It was not until fifteen years after Confederation, in the year 1882, that the first provincial board of health of Ontario was established, this being the first in Canada. Most of the provinces found it in their own interest to collect vital statistics, as the Federal Government failed to undertake this duty, and there gradually developed regular departments of health in the various provinces. This fact, however, does not in law relieve the Federal Government of the duty of administering a public health department. As a matter

of fact, many health services are to-day -conducted by the Federal 'Government Let me enumerate some of them:
Under the Inland Revenue Department: the chief analyst deals with composition of foods and drinks.
The Department of Agriculture: (1) the health conditions of construction camps or public works, controlled by Federal Government; (2) public health of Yukon Territory; (3) disease of animals; (4) various lines of work at Experimental Farm relating to plant and animal life; (5) vital statistics.
Department of Interior: (I) inspection of immigrants; (8) town planning and housing; (3) port hospitals; (4) health of Indians.
Department of Militia and Defence: (1) army medical corps and hospital service;
(2)	sanitation and food for the army.
Department of Public Works r sanitary
inspection of public buildings.
Department of Marine and Fisheries: (1) studies of fish; (8) examination of pilots;
(3)	hospital care of sailors; (4) sanitation of ships; (5) health of sailors; (6) food for the navy.
Post Office Department: (1) sanitation of post offices; (2) infectious diseases as transmitted through mails.
Department of Finance: infectious diseases through handling money.
Department of Justice: (1) sanitation of prisons; (2) diseases of criminals.
These are sufficient to show the various lines of work now being done and the various directions in which expert scientific research will be required in the near future. When, therefore, it is contended that the Federal Government has no power under the British North America Act, we can reply that the Government has for years been taking control of much health work, and when it is asserted that public health is not the duty of the Federal Government under the British North America Act, it can with equal force and logic be insisted that public health is not a function laid upon the provinces since it is nowhere referred to in the Act of Confederation. -i
The present condition in the administration of health matters in Canada is in itself sufficient to warrant the organization of a special department inasmuch as the distribution of this work among eight or ten departments is not conducive to intelligent nor efficient administration. Let me illustrate this by a reference to the methods of dealing with immigrants. Immigrants are inspected by officers of the Department of the Interior. When placed in quaran-

tine they come under control of officers of the Department of Agriculture; and if necessary that ifhigrants be sent to a hospital, they come under officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The results of such a system cannot but be lacking in efficiency.
Canada is almost the only country among the larger nations of the world that has no department of public health, defined as such. Every European country, with the exception of two or three of the smaller states, has a public health service. Japan has a most efficient department, and the United States, although for many years content to leave the administration of health matters chiefly to the individual states, have since 1871 gradually been developing a service under the Federal Government. At the close of the Spanish-Amer-ican war the necessity of an up-to-date service was pressed strongly upon the Federal Government, and in 1902 the public health and marine hospital service was established and provision made for a hygienic laboratory and an advisory board. This board was composed of three competent experts from the army, ,the navy and from the Bureau of Animal Industry, to be associated with the director of the laboratory, and five additional members, to he nominated by the Surgeon General. The Act further provided for establishing research divisions of bacteriology, chemistry, zoology and pharmacology. This organization has made it possible to- provide a large body of trained ofiicials competent in every branch of public health work, not only to carry out the duties laid directly upon them by Congress, but also to be in a position to assist in the study of general problems which might affect the health, prosperity and commerce of the whole American people. In 1912 the duties of the service were further extended, and the whole organized into the Public Health service of the United States, with a surgeon general in charge.
The situations in so far as the Governments are concerned are very similar in both Canada and United States, and the conditions to be met are also so much alike that Canada may well, with the experience of the United -States before her, consider in the light of that experience what her procedure may wisely be.
No duplication of work should be permitted. While the greater part of the health work now done in Canada is undertaken by the municipalities and provinces, the urgent problems of the future are wider than the
mere provincial question; some of them are international. This being the case, it is proper to consider, having in view the changed conditions brought about by the discoveries of science, what is the duty of this Government in the highest interest of health of the whole people of Canada.
I referred a moment ago to the progress in recent years of medical science. Permit me to give some illustrations of this. I need only refer to the discoveries of Pasteur, Koch, Lister, each of whom by his researches, the result of which are known to the whole world, has saved the lives of untold numbers of the human race. Previous to Koch's discoveries, tuberculosis was little understood, and the person who developed the disease faced sure death. But with Koch's remarkable discovery of the tuberculosis bacillus, a new note of hope rang round the world. In the last fifty years the mortality from tuberculosis in Britain has fallen 50 per cent, and there exists to-day in the mind of the student of medical science a sure belief that with time and care tuberculosis will become a rare- disease.
Cuba, which at the time of the Spanish-American war was a plague-stricken land, was,, under the administration of the United States health service, cleared of malaria and typhoid, within a few years of the close of that war, and transformed into one of the garden spots of the world. The greatest thing that the United States has done for Cuba and Porto Rico since the close of the war has been its contribution to those countries of good health and sanitary science.
When the French endeavoured to build the Panama canal their attempts ended in utter failure, owing to the prevalence of disease in that section of our continent, but Surgeon-General Gorgas, by the application of modern science, destroyed the plague-producing agencies and made the construction of this great work a possibility and an assured success.
Our minds are centered to-day upon the great European war, -and it may be interesting to know something about what medical science has done for our armies.
Typhus fever in Scotland in 1865 was responsible for a death rate of 108 per 100,000 of the population. This disease, with its unnumbered tens of thousands of sick and its thousands of dead, has practically vanished in the last fifty years-and its extirpation is a triumph of administration. Typhoid fever, the scourge of armies in previous wars, has, through scientific methods adopted for its control, become in the present war a minor cause of disease in all

armies except those in the Balkans, where sanitation was neglected. The history of smallpox is little less striking. With a death rate in Scotland fifty years ago of 35 per 100,000, it has been reduced until it is less than one per 100,000. With antitoxin, diphtheria has lost its chief terror.
In England and Wales the death rate for the five years from 1861-65 was 21-4 per thousand persons living. From that date the death rate gradually declined, until in 1908 it had fallen to 14-6 per thousand living. Under the improved methods of , medical and sanitary science there was a saving from death of seven persons per each thousand living, or a total saving of
245.000	lives in each year for England and Wales.
Amid all the itumult, amid -cries of anguish and defeat, aanid thunderings of artillery, there stands on the European battle plains the man of science-a -conqueror, undismayed, bringing life and healing to fields of death. He has cut our casualties in two. The bullet has always been a great enemy of human life and Safety, and it has a brother in the bacillus; in fact, the bacillus has generally been -considered a greater enemy th-an the bullet. Disease has been the soldier's deadliest foe. In the Crimea, 6,000 British, 80,000 French and 800,000 Russian soldiers died from fever. In 1870, in the Franco-Prussian war, for every 10 Germans killed, 15 died from disease. In 1877, in the Russo-Turkish war, for every 10 Russians who were killed, 27 died from disease. In Britain's -campaign in Egypt, for 10 British soldiers killed, 42 died from -disease. In the iSpanish-American [DOT] war at one time
20.000	Americans out of an army of
100.000	were ill from typhoid.- In the Boer war, there were 60,000 typhoid cases in the British Army, with 8,000 deaths, -and for every 7 -soldiers killed 'by bullets, 10 were killed by disease. Disease, not cannon, has swept away -the great armies of the past. For years we have had the power to banish half the disease of the world, but we let our power lie idle, and let people die. But war is a great master. It can nationalize railways in an afternoon. It can take over coal mines, close public houses, seize factories. It can take a useless citizen, put him in khaki and make a man of him. So science became clothed with the power of war. While men in the trenches were keeping the -Germans hack, men in the laboratories were keeping back that unseen enemy, disease. The British Army in South

Africa was moTe severely smitten by invisible foes than by all they met in the open. But there was one wise nation, Japan. It remained for her to teach the Governments of Europe how to apply the knowledge they had given to -the world, lapan went to war with science on her side, and for the first time bacilli were less deadly than bullets. There had never been a w-ar with so little typhoid or so few deaths from wounds as the Japanese army which took part- in the Rus-so-Japanese war. [Sir Frederick 'Treves, who observed what happened on that occasion, declared that Russia had been beaten by an English Quaker named Lister. It had been demonstrated that medical science could save men by thousands and tens of thousands, and- at last governments knew it. Admiralties and War Offices knew it; and so it comes about t-hat, for the first time in the history of war, a British army has been equipped against its greatest foe. Science has armed it so effectively that with the greatest British army ever placed in the field, the cases of disease were even less than under conditions of peace. Science makes our soldiers typhoid proof, cholera proof, and tetanus proof. These three enemies are beaten for all time. Under former sanitary and health conditions, and with armies fighting amid the present surroundings, probably typhoid would have claimed 100,000 victims by this time. That it has not is one of the great victories of the war. When all is over, it will be seen that the merciful science developed by France and Britain has saved hundreds of thousands of the lives of the men who are giving their -all to save to the world its civilization and its freedom. If we can conquer disease in war, we can overcome disease in peace; and the nations that have seen what science has wrought in France and in Flanders will be unwilling in years to come to let their people die when they might live. Canada will be one of those nations. These form a minor part of the story of the progress and accomplishments of medical science during recent years and indicate in some small measure what we may expect in the future.
Canada has only begun the business of naition-building, and at this period when the great European war has demonstrated most clearly the advantage of good health among our young men especially, it is opportune that this Parliament should become aroused to the need of devoting more attention to the health of our population, for it

is the physical, mental and moral quality of our people that will establish our position in the world. The future is before us; men of science have afforded us the means of avoiding the errors of the United States and European countries. If we do not build up in this Canada of ours a nation which will surpass physically all others of past history, it will be because of the incapacity and the indifference of the public men of the present day.
Public health is a great social and economic question, one of the most important that any nation has to face at the present day. First, there is the matter of feeblemindedness, so closely associated with immigration which is directly under the control of the Federal Government. At the close of the present war there will undoubtedly be a very large influx of immigrants both from Europe and the United States. It is estimated that in Great Britain there are about three hundred thousand feebleminded. In the United States there are an equal number, rapidly increasing. It is most important, therefore, that the greatest care should be taken in the inspection of our immigrants, as the above figures indicate a fruitful source of supply of mental defectives. It is open to doubt whether our present methods of inspection are all that are required. It seems to me that none but trained experts, qualified for the detection of mental as well as physical ailments, should be in charge of this work.
In 1914-15, 59 immigrants were rejected on account of imbecility, insanity, and mental defect, but in the same year 154 were deported for similar causes; while in the last three years 606 deportations have been made for these causes. Doubtless many of those deported were the offspring of parents whose history, if inquired into in their home lands, would have prevented the immigration to Canada of those deported persons.
To show the prevalence of feeble-mindedness in our country, let me quote the results obtained at a special clinic for feebleminded, conducted by the Toronto General Hospital for twelve months from July 1, 1914, to July 1, 1915. During that time there were discovered 425 feeble-minded persons, of whom 203 were Canadian born and 222 foreign born, showing again that considerable numbers of feeble-minded are gaining admission to our country.
Recently a carefully-conducted examination of 2,064 children in four schools in Toronto by a specialist from the feebleminded clinic of the Toronto General Hospital showed almost four per cent to be
feeble-minded. We have no statistics to show how many mental defectives we have in this country, but it undoubtedly numbers thousands. Someone has said that the greatest menace to race regeneration today is our ever-increasing population of inefficient and feble-minded. Our first duty is to strengthen the inspection of immigrants. A feeble-minded immigrant may in one or two generations cost the state thousands of dollars annually. Let us in this country not repeat the mistakes of the United States, where the care of the insane per annum is costing thirty-two million dollars.
To emphasize the danger to Canada, look at New York State where the authorities havo given the subject more attention than in any other part of America. There are in that state 32,000 feeble-minded in a population of 10,000,000. Of these only 4,900 are cared for. Of the balance, 7,000 are girls and women of child-bearing age, and they are producing children at nearly twice the rate of normal women. A very large percentage of these children will inherit the mental weakness of their mothers and go on adding to the already tremendous burden of providing for the mentally deficient of the state. Let Canada wake up to the threatening danger in this regard; let us profit by the warning given us by New York State.
Infant mortality is another subject which is becoming a great national problem. Our present knowledge of infant life, and the measures taken for the prevention of deaths among infants, guarantee that about 47 per cent of those dying under one year of age could be saved, and that 67 per cent of all diseases that afflict children under five years of age are preventable.
John Burns says: "We are beginning to concentrate on the child." Why should the state spend so much on inducing immigrants to come to our land, and so little in attempts to save our own native born children? Infant sickness and mortality is one of the greatest preventable wastes of to-day. We have in Canada no statistics regarding the economic loss to the nation through sickness of the people but figures from the United States will suggest to us something of our loss.
There are no complete vital statistics collected for the Dominion, the registration of births, marriages and deaths being under provincial control. New Brunswick collects none, and there is no uniform system in the other provinces in the method of collection.
Do I understand the hon. member to say that the United States has a Federal department of health in addition to the state departments?

The United States have a 'most, efficient service-a federal public health service which is under the control of the Federal Government. It was found by the United States that the state boards of health did not meet the full requirements of the nation along these lines.
Let me quote an extract from a book entitled "Health and Disease," written by Dr. W. L. McKenzie, a member of the Local Board of Scotland, in which he says :
It is our duty to prevent death.
That seems like a strong statement, but perhaps it expresses the idea more clearly and succinctly than any other statement could.
It is our duty to prevent death. Out of the effort to keep alive those that would die of preventable diseases, the vast health service has grown. Of what diseases do we die? Of

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) should be congratulated on having brought before this House a subject of very great interest, and he is to be congratulated, also, on the well considered and admirable speech in which he has moved his resolution, a speech that, I am sure, will receive most favourable comment throughout the country, and be of great value in the consideration of this matter. I am sorry that the Minister of Agriculture, within whose department this matter more especially falls, is not able to be present to-day, and, in common with the other members of the House, I more regret the Circumstances which make his presence here impossible on this occasion, because the Minister of Agriculture has given a great deal of thought and careful consideration to this very important subject. If he were present I know he would be able to make an address to the House that would be interesting and illuminating, and that would give far more information than it is possible for me, temporarily filling his position-as I hope for a very short time' only-to do.
The hon. member for South Perth has referred to certain constitutional questions involved in "this subject. I do not think there is any constitutional objection to a department of public health being established by the Dominion Government, either as a separate department or as a branch of one of the departments that at present exist, because, from Confederation down to the present hour, the Parliament of Canada and the Government of Canada have been giving consideration, and have been dealing with questions affecting public health. I think 'it may be fairly said, speaking from a constitutional standpoint, that while there are certain matters in public health, such as quarantines, sick mariners, etc., that come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Federal Parliament, there are many other matters connected with public health over which the Federal Parliament and the provincial parliaments exercise a joint control. The provincial legislatures, for many years past, have be^ji dealing with this subject by law, in practically every province of Canada, Boards of health, provincial and municipal, have been established, and those boards of health have applied themselves, with very excellent results, to the task of improving the sanitary conditions of their communities, and of handling all epidemics of contagious

diseases, such as small-pox, that have arisen from time to time. They have dealt with these matters themselves and have borne the expense of them, and these Acts have been administered by officials appointed under Acts passed by the provincial legislatures.
In addition to that, the provinces of late years have been giving very considerable attention to the question of the prevention of the great white plague, tuberculosis, and in different provinces throughout Canada we find established sanatoria where those who are affected with tuberculosis in its incipient stage can receive treatment, and institutions for those who have passed the incipient stage are being established now in different parts of Canada under legislation passed by the provincial legislatures. In my own province of New Brunswick, a splendid establishment for the cure of incipient cases of tuberculosis is to be found at River Glade, in the county of Westmorland. This institution was established through the generosity of the widow of Mr. Eben Jordan, of the firm of Jordan, Marsh' & Company, of Boston, and it is administered by a commission appointed under an Act passed by the legislature of New Brunswick; Mrs. Jordan being a most valued member of that * commission. In the city of St. John, the municipal authorities have erected an institution for the treatment and possible cure of cases of tuberculosis arising within the city and county of St. John. That institution is carried on * under provincial legislation which provides that the province shall pay a per capita allowance for each patient who is in that sanatorium or in sanatoria of a [DOT]similar character that may be established in different municipalities throughout the province. Similar legislation is to be found in almost all the other provinces.
There is no constitutional objection to the establishment of a department of public health,	but the	question will arise,if such a department should be established, with what subjects connected with public health that department should	deal, so	that it will not
intrench upon what, by practice, has fallen under the jurisdiction of the different provinces, and before any such health 1 department is established, it would be most desirable to consult the different Provincial Governments so that no action may be taken .that would be regarded as tresspassing upon the jurisdiction of the provinces, and upon the work which they feel it is their duty to undertake. As the constitutional question involves considerable interest, I have prepared a statement dealing with what this Dominion has done since Confederation with regard to matters of public health. I find that by chapter 67 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, which created the Department of Agriculture in 1868, immediately after Confederation, the subjects of public health and quarantine were placed under its administration. It. is laid down in chapter "74 of the Revised Statutes of Canada that the administration of quarantine pertains solely to the Dominion Government, so that the precedents established under the British North America Act would lead us to the conclusion that there are certain subjects relating to public health that come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Dominion, and that there are others as to which there is equal control by the Dominion and by the provinces.
Until 1872 the,Quarantine Act contained provisions charging the Department of Agriculture with the administration of publie health, there having been under that department a public health medical board, of which the late Dr. Taehe, Deputy Minister of Agriculture, was the secretary. In 1872, however, the then Minister . of Agriculture, the late Hon. J. H. Pope, advised the elimination of the publie health clauses from the Quarantine Act, because he found that heavy accounts for public health service were presented to him for payment by the provinces while he had no control of appointment or in the direction of the service, which had gradually become provincial. The then premier, Sir John A. Macdonald, concurred in this view, and the Quarantine Act was amended by the elimination of the directory administrative clauses pertaining to public health. The Government of Mr. Mackenzie, which succeeded to office (in 1873) strictly carried out this policy, and did away with the health statistical office at Halifax, which had been retained by the-previous Government.
In 1878, on the return of the ministry of Sir John A. Macdonald to power, Mr. Pope again becoming Minister of Agriculture, on the very earnest representation of Dr. Taehe, the subject of leprosy within the Dominion-which belongs to public health and to which Dr. Taehe had devoted special study on a reference from the Imperial authorities-was again taken over as part of the administration of the department. For many years there has existed in the county of Gloucester in the province of New Bruns<-

wick, and, I believe, to a slight extent in some portions of Nova Scotia, the disease of leprosy, and before Confederation the province of New Brunswick maintained at Tracadie in the county of Gloucester a lazaretto, all the expenses of which were paid by the province. That continued for a short period after Confederation, and then the expenses were borne by the Dominion Government; I believe that the lazaretto was again taken . over by the province, but, in 1878, I find that an arrangement was made with the province of New Brunswick by which the lazaretto at Tracadie was transferred to the Dominion Government, and it has since been administered through the Department of Agriculture. That lazaretto, I may say, has done very excellent work; it has been well managed and well maintained, and the disease i"ith which it is especially intended to cope is gradually though slowly being-eradicated. In addition to this, the Dominion Government from time to time has taken action in isolated cases of leprosy reported within the Dominion and, in late years, more particularly amongst the Chinese in the province of British Columbia.
Under the Canada Shipping Act the care of sick sailors pertains strictly to the subject of public health, and was formerly under the administration of the Department of Agriculture. It is now administered, as hon. gentlemen know, by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, to which it was transferred in virtue of an understanding between the then ministers of the respective departments, the Hon. Mr. Pope and the late Hon. Peter Mitchell. It may further be stated that the practice of the Dominion Government since Confederation has been to take votes for both public health and quarantine.
To sum up, I may say that the administration in all matters pertaining to quarantine, that is the dealing with any infectious disease on its presenting itself at any of the ports of the Dominion, maritime or inland, is vested solely in the Dominion Government; while it is contended that all other matters pertaining to public health are joint between the Dominion and the provinces, in virtue of the provisions of the British North America Act.
There is a Dominion Public Works Health Act, under which sanitary arrangements and matters of that sort in connection with the construction of public works are attended to throughout Canada by the Department of Agriculture.
' Having said that much in a general way

with regard to thd powers of the provinces and of the Dominion with respect to this very important subject, brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for South Perth (-Mr. Steele) I may say that we are all aware that the question of public health is daily assuming greater importance in this country. It has become a distinct subject and branch of study in medical universities throughout the land, and to such an extent is this the case, and it is so recognized as a distinct branch of medical science, that special degrees in public health, for which being now looked universities, including, I believe, the University of McGill, and men who have graduated in public health from these institutions are in some cases acting ' as health officers in different cities of Canada, having been appointed to such positions by virtue of legislation passed by the Provincial Legislatures.
The subject is considered to be of so much importance that the man with the ordinary diploma of M.D. from any university is not regarded as being qualified to deal with the question of public health for which being now looked upon as a special branch of science special degrees are conferred after courses of study.
The progress of hygiene and preventive medicine known under the name of "Public Health " has been rapid and marked, especially during the last few years, and there has undoubtedly been an increasing demand for governmental regulation, In the United States the marine hospital service has been by Act of Congress enlarged into a public health service. There are already departments of public health, I am informed, in some of the sister colonies. There has been discussion about the matter in England, but I do not think the movement for the appointment of a Minister of Public Health, which was very active a few years ago, has been discussed recently, all other subjects, of course, having been made secondary to the problem of the war. The medical profession of Canada speaking through the Canadian Medical Association, has urged the importance of the establishment of a Department of Public Health. The object of the creation of such a department by the Dominion Government, having in view all the subjects related to the public health with which the Government deals at the present time, would, it seems to me, be to consolidate with a view to efficiency and economy in those matters concerning public health and sanitation which are already within the jurisdiction

of the Government, but which are now scattered among the different departments. The question of adding to the duties of a department of public health other matters such as now fall within the control of provincial legislatures, and to which they have been industriously and energetically in many cases giving their attention for years past, will have to be considered carefully, and there would have to be conferences on the subject between the Dominion and, the provinces. The establishment of such a department, it is contended, would obviate the confusion and extra correspondence often caused by the want of knowledge of the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture in public health matters, and would facilitate the business of those who come to the capital in connection with the various sanitary matters now divided up amongst the different offices of the Government, many of them under the direction of non-medical heads, who have little knowledge of medical or sanitary science. That would be a matter of internal domestic consolidation within the Dominion Government itself. It would be a governmental recognition of the importance of public health, and of the authority of such a department to issue rules and regulations on the subject. The experience of the Department of Agriculture, I am informed by its permanent officials, as well as the example of other countries, leads them to believe that such publication so issued would carry much more weight than similar publications issued in the name of any other department.
It may surprise the ftouse to know how many matters affecting public health are dealt with by this Government at the present time. These subjects are now scattered over several departments, without co-ordination or homogeneous supervision, and might well be grouped together in a department of public health:
In the Department of Agriculture:
T. Sanitary advice to Dominion Government.
2.	Quarantine (maritime and frontier.)
3.	Leprosy throughout the Dominion.
4.	Public Works Health Act.
5.	The sanitary part of the census.
6.	Vital statistics (Dominion).
7.	Health of animals.
8.	Inspection of meats and canneries, and factories of foods generally.
In the Department of Inland Revenue:
9.	Adulteration of foods and drugs.

Also	.
13.	Supervision of sanitary measures and sanitary police in the Territories which have no organization corresponding to a Provincial Board of Health.
14.	National bacteriological laboratory.
A department of public health could be equipped with a national bacteriological laboratory, as is the case in other countries. Such a laboratory could report promptly on suspected specimens of micro-organisms from vessels, trains, etc., held under quarantine of observation. The quality and purity of the various protective and curative agents, such as vaccine, tuberculine, Haff-kine's prophylactic plague fluid, and the anti-toxins and serums of plague, cholera, diphtheria, typhoid, anthrax, etc., are of the utmost importance to the public health and to the well being of the country. It is suggested that the manufacture of these protective and curative agents might be carried on by salaried officials in the national laboratory, and the issue of them could be under the supervision and direction of the proposed public health department. In this way, it is claimed, the maximum protection of the people of Canada in this matter can alone be attained and that confidence secured which will induce the people to properly avail themselves of these all-important means of protection from epidemic and infectious disease. It is also contended that in such a national laboratory here might well be bacteriologists and chemists engaged in original research. This country would thus rise above the position of hanging on to the skirts of other nations and waiting to hear from them of the progress made in these important lines of science. Other people have suggested additional subjects that might be included if a department of public health is esablished. After conferences with the various provinces, the following might be included:
15.	Sanitary direction of the service of protection of international waterways-a most important subject.
1C. Sanitary supervision of the protection of the public health against tuberculosis, a subject that is being dealt with on a large scale by several of the provinces.
17. Smallpox and vaccination.
That, I understand, is already dealt with

by the Dominion Government. In case oi a smallpox epidemic along the border, the Dominion Government takes means to see to it that the people are vaccinated and the spread of the disease prevented while the local authorities take steps to quarantine the disease in the different cities and towns and to isolate people who have contracted the disease.
18. Railroad, car and steamboat sanitation, a most important matter-to see to the disinfection of cars, and public conveyances, in order to assure the exclusion of malignant microbes so that disease may not be spread by those who travel.
There is already an official of the Government known as the Director General oi Public Health and Sanitary Adviser of the Dominion Government, with the rank of deputy minister. But, up to the present, the matters I have enumerated have been left scattered through the different departments and not collected under the control of a specially qualified officer. I presume that their union, co-ordination and development would naturally follow the creation of such a department.
As I said at the outset, I regret that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) is not here, because I know that in the last few years he has given a great deal of thought and study to this very important subject. My hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele) has undoubtedly accomplished a good work in bringing this matter to the attention of the House. It will no doubt attract attention throughout the country, and will cause the public to give consideration to this important matter. And, while, at the present moment, our thoughts are taken up with the war now being waged, and upon which our liberties and the institutions of our country depend, to the exclusion of practically every other subject, yet I think that all will agree that the time occupied by the House this afternoon in a discussion of this matter, so well brought to our attention by the hon. member for South Perth, is time not wasted. I would suggest to my hon. friend that it would not be desirable to cause the resolution to be pressed to a vote this afternoon. I can assure him that the matter will receive, as it has received, the best thought and attention of the Government. I am sure that when the Minister of Agriculture is once more restored to health and able to deal with the work of his department he will be only too glad to pursue the study which he has been giving to this matter, that in future it may receive the considera-

tion, and I trust the action, that its importance deserves.

This, in my judgment, is one of the most important questions to come under the consideration of this House, and I regret that I did not know that the motion was to be up for discussion this afternoon. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) who has charge of the department under which this arises, and who has given the subject special consideration, is not here, and for that reason, and because I know that, besides myself, there are a number of medical men, members of the House, who would like to present some ob-

subtopic: FRENCH CANADIANS IN THE CIVIL SERVICE OF CANADA.
FRENCH CANADIANS IN THE CIVIL SERVICE OF CANADA.
speechtext:
(Translation) moved,
That, in the opinion of this House, Canadians of the French language should hold positions in the employ of the Intercolonial Railway, and in the public service of Canada, in proportion to their number in the country; and that it is urgent and in the public interest that all civil servants holding higher offices, and drawing salaries of $2,000 and oyer, should understand the two official languages of this country, and that no official in the said service should be admitted into the Civil Service in future unless he can fulfil such conditions.
He said: (Translation). Mr. Speaker, There are two distinct parts to this motion; the first refers to the employees on the Intercolonial railway, the other one states that the higher officials in the Civil Service, those belonging to Class A and first subdivision A of Class B, should speak the two official languages of this country.
As to the first part, namely, that concerning the Intercolonial, I have many times in past years, drawn the attention of the House to the injustice done the Freneh-Can-adians and French-Acadians, who are not treated as their number would warrant. That state of things has been in existence for the last forty-four years.
French speaking Canadians seem to have been completely ignored, or nearly so, on the whole system of the Intercolonial.
Notwithstanding repeated requests on my part and numerous articles in French publications we have always met with difficulties that should not exist, especially when the facts are called to the attention of the authorities.

Last fall, Le Progres <hi Golfe had an article, dealing partly with our grievances, which I intend reading, so that it may be of record in Hansard. It read as follows:
French Canadians and the Intercolonial.
Some newspapers published in English complain that French Canadians are not enlisting at a sufficient rate in the ranks of those who are going to the battlefield of Europe to be scorched alive.
The charge is groundless. If only the proportion were properly computed, it would be seen that the native .English Canadians who have enlisted are not more numerous than the French-Canadians. It must be kept in mind that a large number of English recruits come to Canada to enlist, likely to obtain a higher salary, but they are Englishmen and not Canadians, as may be seen by the daily newspaper bulletins.
If the English-Canadians received the same treatment as French-Canadians in Canada's Civil Service they would be less anxious than ourselves to rally to the colours. In fact, were we not moved by our feelings of sympathy for blood-bespattered Belgium, were we not connected with France by the sacred ties of blood, were not with Great Britain, which has always treated us in all fairness, entitled to our gratitude, and were we to consider solely the treatment meted out to us by the English speaking population in Canada, not one French-Canadian should be found at the front.
Why? We are systematically debarred from every public employ ; we are treated as outcasts and slaves, all the best-paying offices in the country are closed to us, there being nothing left for the French-Canadian but the small salaries and the positions as snow-shovellers and messengers; how may we in return be anxious to get killed at the bid of those gentlemen who flay us alive?
Our national pride, inherited of old from France, revolts every day against the injustices we are made to suffer. And why protest? Our English-speaking fellow-citizens are in resolve bound to allow to French-Canadians a bare twentieth part of what they are entitled to. That crying injustice has been in existence of old; it is continued from decade to decade, and the present generation of Englishmen is nothing loath to -take our places and crush us under heel. Here and there, a sympathetic Englishman may be found whose feelings towards us are sincerely generous, but the number of such is so small that their voice is not listened to. I shall point out one case in a thousand that happened on the Intercolonial. The section from Mont-Joli to Campbellton is 105 miles in length, of which 3,2 miles run through the province of Quebec. All along the railway, the population is French-speaking. Although situated in the province of Quebec, not one of the superior officials of that section of the line speak a word of French. There is a superintendent, an assistant, a chief train despatches four other train despatches, a bridge foreman, four line foremen, a divisional engineer, all high-salaried officers, not a single one of whom is a FrenCh-Canadian. One of them has within the past two years learned to speak a little French, and the intention, it seems, is to put in his place an employee who cannot understand us.
Should men be wanted for some important work, French-Canadians are hired for the heavy work, but the foreman and even the timekeepers are always English-speaking who cannot understand the men. Even foremen are appointed
of the stamp of a certain Bulmer who writes articles in tAe Orange Sentinel against our language and our faith.
During last fall, a vacancy occurred in the position of superintendent on the section from Moncton to Mont-Joli, when I saw that the illness of the superintendent was likely to prove fatal, I set to work to notify the railway authorities that in case of a vacancy caused by the expected death of Mr. Price, the French-speaking Canadians would ask the appointment of a French superintendent. That cannot be denied either by the Minister of Railways or by the general manager, because I took the trouble to interview those officers and explain to them the situation. Some of my friends also wrote more strongly in support of my re- . quest that justice be done to the French-Canadians.
The facts show that our efforts failed. Yet' candidates for the vacancy were not wanting. I suggested a number of names, among others, that of a man who has been on the Intercolonial during thirty years of his life and who was dismissed for the bare reason that he was a Conservative. He was entitled, from all viewpoints, to the gratitude of his party, on account of both his personal qualifications and his services on the Intercolonial. His name is Rodolphe Blais.
I also suggested names of many others whose qualifications could not be impeached.	.
What was the result?-A man has been appointed by the name of Davenish, who hails from Ulster, and who has been a year or two on the Transcontinental and only one year in the offices of the Intercolonial at Moncton.
I felt sorry, lately, to hear the answer of the acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) to the question asked by the hon. member for Bonaventure.

Mr. Marcil:
1.	Who succeeded the late Mr. Price as Superintendent ot the Intercolonial railway, at Campbellton?
2.	Was the principle of promotion followed in the appointment?
3.	Was the new appointee connected with the Intercolonial railway service?
Mr. Reid:	,
1.	W. R. Devenish.

Peculiar promotion that, when the highest appointment on the Intercolonial goes to foreigners who know nothing of the railroad, the employees or the travelling public!

What? You call it a promotion when a man is appointed who has only one year's experience on the railway?
He was appointed over the heads of old employees, who, a great number of whom began as mere labourers at small salaries; and how many among them would be glad to earn those fat stipends paid by the railway to those foreign officials.
Instead of an attempt being made to encourage the employees who properly >
perform their duties, they are debarred from any promotion. One might think that they are expected to do the bare work that their salary pays for.
That particular state of things is not specially of this Government's doing, as I pointed out in another article published in Le Progres du Golfe last November, -but this treatment of the employees has been prevalent since 1896, at which time strangers were invited from all over, to take the place of those higher officers who were found to be too Conservative.
I claim that in all justice, such should not be the case, and that if it be a shame for common employer of labour to act thus unfairly, it is still more so for the (Government, who ought, to set the example of fair treatment and justice.
When the new superintendent was to be appointed, a few suggested for the vacancy the name of the member for Rimouski and Matane.
The Hon. the Minister of Railways -quickly replied that the Government's policy was not to give appointments to members, and that moreover an officer in a position of such importance required in the interest of the public certain definite qualifications. I shall first state that I have never directly or indirectly sought the position, and had it been offered me, I .should have refused it; and secondly I wish to tell the Hon. the Minister of Railways that I pretend to know as much as he about railway administration, since I have been connected with it almost all my life, by my intercojirse both with the employees and the management.
Let us now revert to the reasons I gave at that time in support of my request for the appointment of a JFrench-Canadian superintendent.

All those employees are supposed to be men of especial ability, and to be paid by the country, according to their qualifications and their education. But, any among them who speak no other lnaguage but English, are not in a position to properly perform their duties, when they are called on to meet citizens who speak French only or vice versa, supposing those higher officials were French-speaking and had, now and then, intercourse with Englishspeaking members of parliament or citizens. Those gentlemen have to travel throughout the country in the interest of their department, and, as for us, in the province of Quebec, we have to deplore the fact that those who are acquainted with nothing but English are of no practical benefit. Let us, as an instance, take the higher officials of the Agriculture Department. They have to impart their practical knowledge by means of lectures delivered, not only to the English population, but to the French people as well. I do not remember ever seeing them in the county of Rimouski, where, in any case, their presence would be of no practical avail, so far as their giving useful information, since they would not be understood by most of the farmers. That is altogether unfair to French-Canadians who speak no English, for they are called upon to pay their share of the salaries of those officials equally with the English-speaking farmers.
I have no objection to the lower grade of civil servants speaking only the language they choose. But, as regards higher officers, I strongly insist on a complete reform being made. It is a common thing for some of us among the members to go into an office where in a staff of a dozen employees, none are found to understand our French. See what would happen to a farmer from Quebec who could not speak English. If at least the head of the depart- -ment spoke French, we should at any rate get from him the information sought. Such a regulation would also result in all those who aim at the higher appointments having to study the two official languages, a boon indeed to both English-speaking and French-speaking people. The first question a French applicant for a position at Ottawa has to answer is: Do you know English? Why, even here, in the House of Commons, we are unfairly dealt with. There are twelve young pages, and only three of them speak French. In the office for the distribution of Hansard, although the officer has beeii changed three times since 1911, in each case the position went to a man who could not understand a word of French. And most of the employees of the House who are of English origin do not speak a word of French.
If my suggestion were put into practice, we should learn to know ourselves better, to appreciate one another better, and my remarks apply not only to the English provinces, bu't as well to what takes place in my own province.
I remember that in my young days, every one in my parish held everything English in high detestation. Brought up with that idea, we came to college strongly determined to speak nothing but French, and the teachers met with all kinds, of difficulties, and generally failed to make us understand how important was to us a knowledge of English. Most of our educational institutions of the province of Quebec turn out graduates who can neither speak nor write English. Only later, when they have to do their share in the struggle for life, do they see the awful mistake they made in neglecting the study of such an important language. .
It must be acknowledged that conditions even worse prevail in the English provinces, where I must say the French language is completely ignored. People have the idea that it will never be of any use to them. If students were made to see as they enter school, that in order to secure certain important positions in Canada or become somebody, they must learn the two pfficial languages, I "feel sure that, first of all, the teachers would find them less refractory to learning a second language, and secondly, the students themselves would later realize how beneficial it has become 'to them.
As a result of a general knowledge of both languages, we should become less averse to each other, because the fact stands that, in certain quarters, there are between the two races feelings of distrust

and aversion. I grant that a number of people are to be found, with a wider and more patriotic outlook, \yho are above those petty jealousies, and will readily give each one his due, whether French or English. But they do not form the bulk of our population. Let us get rid of our blinding fanaticism; let us study the two official languages of the country, and I feel sure that the first step will have been taken towards an era of peace and happiness, unprecedented in Canada.
When both languages become necessary in order to reach the most remunerative positions in the gift of the Government, the tyrannical legislation which seeks to bar French from the schools in the English provinces will gradually disappear, the present agitation will cease and there will come to exist the same conditions as prevail in Quebec: complete freedom in education for both races..
Let us also suppress papers such as The *Sentinel, and put a stop to the furious attacks made against our faith and our language, and complete harmony will he restored among all classes of citizens.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

It is his duty not to allow his preferfence to be seen.
If enlistment seems to be going slower in Quebec than in the other provinces- which I am not prepared to grant-the English and French fanatics in this country are responsible for it. Let us have justice throughout Canada. We want very little after all: only the right of teaching our language, of educating our children as we desire, of receiving our share of the public offices, and no more. We do not want to hamper the teaching of English in Canada, ' far from it. Let it be taught everywhere. We say that our British connection is the FrenchJCanadians' best safeguard. We are not annexationists. We desire to remain-. Canadians and inhabit the land we have inherited from our ancestors. If we are to be denied that legitimate request for freedom, if we are, not to be treated on an equal footing with all the other citizens of this ' country, better know our fate once for all, so that we may ask without delay the repudiation of the Federal pact, which would not then have for us the value of the scrap of paper on which it is written. The destruction of individual freedom will always entail endless controversies, going even to' the shedding of blood. If justice is not to be ours, let it be known now, and we are willing to see the province of Quebec withdraw from Confederation. It is not our desire, of course, to pass under any other domination buit the British Crown, nor, become one of the United States, but we must have complete and absolute freedom.
The few remarks I have made are not prompted by any bitterness or secret design; their only purpose is to point out the conditions in which we are placed, and I hope my intentions have been clearly grasped by the statesmen who sit in this House and are called upon, each in his own sphere, to enlighten public opinion. The teaching of French properly is no danger to public morality. One may easily judge of its moral effect from a comparison of the two races. The Citizen of Ottawa, edited in English, admitted that in the province of Quebec, crime was much less prevalent than in the English provinces.
If such be the case-and there is no doubt of it-there can then be no harm in practising the Catholic faith and teaching the French language and I trust that the greater fanatics among our friends will grant that my words are perfectly true.
I would now like to say a few words in English, so that my fellow members who 
speak that language may understand what I have said, and I hope they will admit that I am right. The first part of the resolution refers to the employees on the Intercolonial railway. For forty years the Intercolonial railway has been running through the province of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, and I claim that the French speaking population of these provinces have not had their share of patronage on that railway. I have given a list that will show my fellow members that I am- right in what I say. The French speaking population in the Maritime Provinces and in the province of Quebec are perfectly justified in claiming their rights. Of the population along the Intercolonial railway, particularly between Moncton and Mont-Joli, 66 per cent are French, and 34 per cent English, but instead of the number of French speaking employees being according to the population, they number only 20 per cent.
In the second part of the resolution, I refer to the CiviJ, Service of Canada, and particularly to the employees in the higher grades, those whose duties render it necessary for them to come in contact with the French speaking population, or with the French speaking members of this House while in attendance at Ottawa. It refers to the employees who, by reason of the fact that they cannot speak French, are unable to give satisfaction. It often happens that when a French Canadian member enters one of the departments, he finds a staff of from ten to twelve employees, none of whom can understand him. The resolution does not refer to employees of the lower grades, but simply to those who are paid large salaries, from $2,000 to $5,000 a year, and these I maintain should be men possessing a knowledge of the French language, so as to be fully equipped for their positions, and to give satisfaction, not only to the English speaking people of this country, but also to the French speaking population. Take the men for instance at the head of the Department of Agriculture. They are called upon to attend conferences in various parts of the country, and to direct the development of agriculture throughout the country, but so far as the French speaking population is concerned, they are practically of no use, because of their lack of knowledge of the French language. Men with less knowledge could fill their places just as well at smaller salaries. The French speaking population cannot profit from their services at all. When they go into the province of Quebec, the people, except in a few centres, cannot understand them. I maintain that the employees of the Civil Service ' occupying the

higher positions should know both the official languages of this country.
In closing these remarks, I may express the hope that they will be accepted in the best spirit. I am not actuated by any animosity or hatred; I simply wish my fellow countrymen to understand the situation. It is not only in connection with the school question that there is a kind of animosity, if I may use that term, between the two great races in Canada. The feeling does not start there; it started at Confederation, and perhaps before Confederation. We feel that we have never been treated as fairly as we should have been. We do not want to do injustice to anybody, but we want fair play, and when we get that, our English speaking countrymen will find that we will cease to grumble.

Mr. Speaker, I should like this evening to say a few words in support of the resolution moved by my hon. friend, the member for Rimouski, but as the Minister of Railways is ill and Dr. Reid, who take his place could not reach the House on account of the storm, I think it better to move to adjourn the debate.
