speakeroldname: Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY (St. John city) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that the Government should promote legislation to amend The Dominion Elections Act, so as to provide that upon any province/ of Canada enacting legislation giving women the right to vote for members of the Provincial Legislature, such women as are on the Provincial voters lists, or as are otherwise entitled to vote for members of the Legislature in such province, shall also, unless otherwise disqualified, have the right to vote at elections for members of this House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is now nearly thirty years since I had the honour of proposing in the Provincial Legislature of New Brunswick a resolution to grant to women the right of suffrage. I had made that question an issue at the polls in the county for which I was a candidate, and I was elected. The people approved of my stand, but the resolution which I proposed was defeated in the Legislature by a small majority, and although the resolution was largely supported, the proposed measure never became law. Entertaining the views which I did at that time, that it was proper to grant to women the right of voting, and not having seen any occasion since to change those views, it is particularly gratifying to me at
the present time to know that a Bill has already passed the Legislature of Manitoba granting equal suffrage to women, and that at the opening of the session of the Alberta Legislature, it was declared in the speech from the Throne that one of the principal measures which the Government would submit would be a Bill granting female suffrage. I have the Edmonton Bulletin, which contains the speech of the Lieutenant Governor of Alberta, and I find in it the following paragraph:
For many years there has been a growing feeling that the equality of the sexes should be recognized, and that the women, who, perhaps in a special degree in a new country, have aided in the development, put up with the hardships and assisted in the prosperity, should have the right to take an equal part in the Government of the country. My Government has considered this question, and has decided that so far as the legislature has power, this equality should in Alberta be fixed by law, and that for the future there should be no distinction of sexes in our province.
I think that declaration reveals the spirit which should animate the members of legislatures in the other provinces of Canada, as well as the members of this Parliament.-For my part, I do not see that one supporting the proposition of equal suffrage is called upon to present any arguments in -its favour, because I think that the burden should rest entirely upon those who oppose the granting of this measure of justice. I am unable to see one reasonable argument that can be presented against granting to the women of our country the same right to -share in public affairs, the same Tight to vote for members of the legislatures, or of Parliament, as is granted to the male portion of the community. But, with respect to the. resolution which I have ventured to submit for the opinion of this House, it is not necessary, I think, that one should declare in the abstract in favour of granting female suffrage and for this reason: when the Liberal party came into power in 1896, there was then upon the statute book an Act providing for a federal franchise and providing federal machinery for the making up of the lists of voters and for the qualification of voters. The Liberal Government took office, and at a very early period it carried through Parliament a measure doing away with the Federal Franchise Act and making provision that the provincial lists in the various provinces, and the law providing the -qualification of voters, should govern in federal elections as well. During the whole of the period while tiie Liberal party was in power.



that principal was adhered to. The Conservative party has now been in office governing this country for upwards of four years, and no move has been made to change the present Dominion Elections Act. So, I think we may fairly take it for granted that both parties in this country are agreed that whatever may be the qualification for voters for the provincial legislatures in the different provinces, shall also be the law in so far as the right of electors to vote for the Dominion House of Commons is concerned.
It will be observed that my resolution only proposes that the Government should frame legislation to provide that in those provinces where the right of suffrage has been granted to women by the legislatures, women in those provinces shall have the right to vote at elections for members of the House of Commons. The necessity for making some such provision, I think, will be abundantly clear from an examination of the Dominion Elections Act. An examination of the provisions of the Revised Statutes of Canada, Volume 1, chap. 6, shows that in respect to all of the provinces, except Alberta, Saskatchewan, and the Yukon Territory, there is no express prohibition of women voting.

There is no prohibition in Saskatchewan against the ladies voting.
Mr. PU'GSLEY:	There is, unless the
law has been changed recently.
They voted there in 1912.
For the Dominion?
No, for the provincial legislature:

I am speaking now of elections for the Dominion House. There is no express prohibition in the Dominion Elections Act against women in that part of Canada other than Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Yukon, voting for the Dominion House of Commons, and it might be very well argued that if, in that part of the Dominion which is not embraced within Alberta, Saskatchewan, and the Yukon Territory women'weTe placed upon the provincial voters' lists they would have the right to vote in Dominion elections. But, when we bear in mind that also in respect to the representation in this Parliament there is no prohibition against women, and that the statute is equally silent in regard to women sitting in this House as it is in regard to women ' voting for members, I think, perhaps, it would raise a very strong
[Mr. Pug-sley.l
doubt as to whether or not, if the question came before the courts, it would be held that women have the right to vote, merely because there is no express prohibition of their exercising that right. The words of the statute with regard to candidates for Parliament are simply that a British subject may ibe elected to Parliament. The words will be found in 'Section 69:
Except as in this Act otherwise provided, any British subject may_be a candidate in an election for a seat in the House of Commons.
These words-, of course, are broad enough to allow a woman, if she is a British subject, to be elected to this House. The same argument, which could be made in favour of giving isuch ia construction to the provisions of the Act which relate to the rest of Canada, apart from Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Yukon as would give to women the right to vote for members of Parliament would also give women the right to sit as members of Parliament. I doubt very much if the statute would be so interpreted by the courts.
My hon. friend the, Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) knows that some years ago, in the province of New Brunswick, an application was made 'by a lady for admission to the Bar. There was no prohibition in the provincial statute against women practising at the Bar, and therefore there would have been, on the face of the statute, apparently no reason why a woman should not be -admitted to practise law. But, when the question came before the courts on application for a mandamus to compel the Barristers' Society to admit a lady to the practice of the law, the court determined that as from time immemorial women had not been allowed to practise, or had not practised either at the Bar in Great Britain or in New Brunswick, it had not been the intention of the legislature -to grant that privilege in the	absence of express
language of the statute granting it. Assuming that decision to be correct, I should judge that a similar argument might be made in respect to women being elected members of this House, namely that from time immemorial women had not been permitted to be elected as members of the British House of Commons or of this Parliament, and therefore were not eligible. It would, I fear, be held that when this Legislature passed the Dominion Elections Act it had not in mind the giving to women of the right to vote. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) informs me that a similar

case arose in respect to an application of women to study law in the province of Quebec. In one portion of Canada, there is an express prohibition against women voting for members of Parliament. Part two of the Dominion Elections Act, consisting of sections 32 and 33 says:
In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta except, as in this Apt otherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act, who, not being an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years and has resided-
Then follows the provision for residence. There is the same prohibition in respect of the Yukon territory in section 33:
In the Yukon Territory, save as in this Act ptherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act, who, not being an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years.
Then again by the form of the proclamation which will be found upon page 82 of volume 1, revised statutes; and which is made a part of the statute there is this notice for the electors:
The following is the qualification of electors as prescribed by Parliament:
In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory except as in this Act otherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act, who, not being an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years and has resided in the provinces of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Yukon territory, as the case may be, for at least 12 months.
And then in the oath, which will be found on page 89, in case the right of any one to vote is challenged, the oath is as follows:
Do you swear you are of the male sex and a British subject, that you are not an Indian, that you are of the full age of 21 years and have resided in the provinces of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Yukon territory, as the case may be, for at least 12 months.
What Act is my hon. friend quoting?
The Dominion Elections Act. ,
There have been some changes.	'
I have not been able to find any revisions of these sections; they have not been altered buit remain in the statute.

My hon. friend should
look up the Saskatchewan Act and he will find in it some very important changes.
751	.
That would be so far as the Saskatchewan Legislature is concerned.
The same law applies in Saskatchewan to the Dominion and to the provincial elections.

My hon. friend is wrong. The Legislature would make provision for the lists, but this Parliament has never altered those provisions of the statute which expressly limit the right to vote to males. Parliament has' not changed the law in that respect. I am quite aware that the Legislature of Saska/tchewan has made provision for electoral lists and, as a reasonable consequence, one would suppose that apart altogether from this question having arisen, this Parliament would have followed the action of the Legislature of Saskatchewan and made in regard to that province similar provisions to those which exist in other provinces where there are lists.
Surely my hori. friend would not ask us to follow Saskatchewan, when they provided that it was not necessary to be a British subject to exercise the franchise in that province.

I should think myself that the right of franchise should be limited either to British subjects or to those who have taken the statutory declaration. Perhaps my hon. friend might be able to point me to that statute.
I shall be delighted.
Since the fire we are at a great disadvantage in getting books of reference.

The Minister of Public Works is a little bit wrong. There was a question whether the Saskatchewan Act stated definitely that the voter had to be a British subject, but that was removed by amendment in the session after the question arose.
Following an election.
In Saskatchewan we do not use the provincial lists in Dominion elections.
I thank my hon. friend from Assiniboia for the statement he has made. I have no doubt the minister made his statement in perfect good faith.
My statement is perfectly correct.
I have no doubt the minister is glad to have the information from the hon. member for Assiniboia.
There is no information that changes my statement at all.

At all events, this does not at all militate against my statement that this Parliament has not yet taken away the disqualification on female residents of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the- Yukon, and I care not what may be the legislation of the provinces, until this Parliament chooses to legislate these sections which I have read are in force and must necessarily govern the returning officers, and must necessarily determine the right to vote, so far as sex is concerned.
Would it not be well for my hon. friend to amend his resolution and make it applicable to all parts of Canada?

If I were to do that it would raise in a broader way the question of the right of suffrage, and it would be changing the provincial lists. If the law were changed in accordance with the suggestion of my hon. friend, the result would be that in all the provinces where female suffrage has not been adopted there would have to be two lists.
I should think the provinces would be very glad to follow the example of this Parliament if we should adopt it.

I am not sure that this Parliament has decided that it will be governed by the .views of the Provincial Legislature in this respect. I did not think it wise to make the resolution so broad as my hon. friend suggests, and, further, I did not deem it desirable to do so in this Parliament because we have it on record, if the right hon. the Prime Minister is reported correctly, that ih an interview which took place recently between a committee representing the women of Canada who are in favour of female suffrage, and himself, when the Government was pressed to promote legislation along the lines now suggested by the Minister of Public Works, the Prime Minister stated that the Government could not deal with the matter because it was one entirely for the legislatures of the different provinces. The Prime Minister is quite correct in that statement because, as long as Parliament says that the franchise shall be defined by toe legislatures of the provinces, and that toe provincial lists shall be the lists upon

which elections for the Dominion shall be held, we cannot properly depart from the franchise as it may be laid down in the different provinces by the provincial legislatures. The House will at once recognize how anomalous it would be that in Manitoba, which has given to women the right to vote, they might have the right to vote for members of this House, that is, on the theory that there is no direct prohibition in Manitoba, and in the province of Saskatchewan they would be denied that right by reason of the express prohibition which is in the Dominion Elections Act.
It is in our power to correct that.

Yes. That was my
object in bringing this matter before the House to-night, not in any partisan spirit, but simply with a view to getting an expression of opinion from the House, and with a view to having the Government act so that there may be no question as to the right of women to vote in those provinces in respect to which the right to vote in a provincial election is granted to them.
Would the hon. member be willing to go as far as the legislature of Manitoba did and extend the franchise to include the right of women to occupy seats in this Parliament?

My hon. friend can answer that question for himself. It is not involved in my motion and it will be time enough to consider it when the question arises. I am not at all disposed to fear that any harm will come to the province of Manitoba by reason of women being given the right to sit in the legislature and take part in the government of Canada. I think they have that right in New Zealand and Sweden.
And Norway. ,

I know they have it in a large number of the states of the Union, and I have never heard that any harm has come to the people of those countries or states by reason of women having been given the right to sit in the legislatures.
During the terrible eighteen months through which this Empire has passed, the women of this country have shown that they are just as loyal and that they know their duty just as well as the men, and that they can make the same necessary sacrifices in the interest of the country and of the Empire. In England they have shown their willingness and ability to take

the place of the men in the workshops and to engage in those various avocations to which it was supposed before that men were specially adapted, and in which it was supposed that women had no place. By their, conduct during this war the women of this country have earned the right to be recognized as the equals of men and to be given the opportunity of discharging equally with men those duties which pertain to citizenship in a free country. That is the answer which I make to my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), and if he or anyone else will move that women should be given the right to sit in Parliament, I can assure him that he will have, in the person of myself, a sympathetic listener to his arguments. I am inclined to think that the motion which I am making to-night will be received with hearty approval by my constituents. I am only asking this Government to promote legislation which will carry out what has been the view of this Parliament for the past nineteen years, that is, that the provincial lists of voters in the different provinces shall govern in the elections in those provinces for members of this Parliament. This legislation is necessary in order to remove difficulties and make the provincial lists really and truly the lists for the election of members of Parliament, and to place all the provinces, which from time to time may grant women suffrage, in the same position so far as electing members to the House of Commons is concerned. It is not necessary for me to argue the general question, because the events of recent years, the trend of legislation in . other countries, the benefits which have accrued to those countries which have adopted woman suffrage, all tend to throw, and ought to be sufficient to throw the onus upon those who would seek to oppose such a measure as this which is manifestly founded upon the principles pf justice and equal rights to all the members of the community.

Mr. Speaker, while it is a common practice m this House, when a mere academic resolution is proposed,, to have it disposed of either by an adjournment so as to place a further discussion of it beyond the possibility of being reached during the session in which the motion is made, or by a vote being taken upon it as a mere matter of form, I do not intend to sit silent until the matter proposed by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is disposed cf. I
desire at the earliest possible moment to put myself on record, in language as concise and clear as I may command, as being against the principle enunciated, in the resolution.
My hon. friend has stated that the onus is upon those who oppose woman suffrage to show that they should not be permitted the right to vote in Federal elections. It will not be very difficult to give reasons why the reception which the proposal to give women the right .to vote received in the states of Massachusetts. New Jersey, and New York a few months ago ought to be accorded to the present resolution by representatives occupying seats in this House. I am opposed to the resolution of the hon. member for St. John because it refers only to a franchise to be exercised by women in the, province of Manitoba. This Parliament ought not to be asked to legislate piecemeal with respect to those who shall have the right to vote in Federal elections. I cannot understand why the women of the province of Manitoba, estimable and intelligent though they may be, shall have the right to vote in Federal elections, while the women of the other provinces are excluded from that privilege. We are legislating here, not for one province alone, not for one section of the Dominion, but for the whole of Canada, and any proposal or resolution designed to give the people, either male or female, certain privileges in any particular portion of Canada ought not to prevail unless those rights and privileges are made applicable throughout the Dominion.
The demand for woman suffrage is made because women claim to be the equal of men in all respects, and that is one of the arguments put forward by the hon. member for St. John. For my part I never dispute the proposition that women are not only equal, but in many respects, superior to men; but does it add to their superiority, or does it increase their virtues to accord to them the privilege of voting and becoming a part and parcel of the political machinery of this country? The right to vote is only one prilivege which is sought to be conferred upon women by this proposed legislation. Although women are the equal of men in this country, there are certain positions which men occupy which are not occupied by women, although they are not prevented from occupying them by reason of any hostile or adverse legislation. In this country there are large railway corporations, banking institutions, and industrial corporations which are governed by men alone. There is not a railway, bank-

ing, or industrial corporation in this Dominion on whose board of directors women sit. Now, is that because there is any legislation, or any lack of legislation, which prevents them from 'sitting there? There is no reason in the world why the good women of this country should not occupy positions on these boards of directors, but they do not, and I have not heard of any great agitation on the part of our estimable women to be accorded seats upon these boards. I presume that the reason why we have no agitation with respect to that is that it is not necessary to come to Parliament in order to have these rights accorded. It appears to me folly to say that women are excluded from the right to vote in this country because they iare not assumed to be the equal of <men. As I ipointed out, there are other responsible and important positions in this country in which women could take their seats beside men, and have not done so up to the present time. I do not understand that there is any particular reason why these positions should not be occupied by women unless it is that these large corporations have been managed from the beginning by men and have (been .made successful by the business energy and pluck put into them by .men. It may also be because the wealth of this country, like the wealth of all countries of the civilized world, has been, produced by men, women not having participated to the same extent in adding to the wealth which makes these corporations possible. These may be the reasons why women have not put themselves forward as entitled to participate in the management of these institutions.
The demand is also made that women should have the right to vote because there should be no taxation without representation. The right to vote will not give these women representation. I am opposed to the resolution of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) because if it were accepted by the House it would not settle anything. The right to vote is only one of the rights which, if that be granted, must be .accorded to women. My hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx) I think hit the nail upon the head when he asked the hon. member for St. John if he is willing to concede to women the right to sit in Parliament. The influence of electors is very small in matters of taxation. Tom Jones or John Brown, living in a Temote district in Nova Scotia, has v*ery little influence on the Finance Minis-
ter in settling his Budget. In order to give representation to which one is entitled who is subject to taxation, it must be given not in the electoral list but on the floor of Parliament. But there are certain advantages and rights which women enjoy by reason of any taxation they pay quite equal to those enjoyed by men. In the matter of civic taxation, women who have property have the same police protection, the .same enjoyment of municipal regulations to protect their property, as the men have. On the other hand, hon. gentlemen who occupy seats in the other branch of this Parliament, though they are considered intelligent men, possessing considerable wealth in some instances, have no right to say in what manner taxation shall be levied upon them. We have there a case of taxation without representation.
It is stated by the advocates of woman suffrage that women are [DOT] entitled to vote because it would give them an opportunity to exercise their influence with respect to matters pertaining to property and civil rights. Now, property and civil rights are matters concerning which this Parliament has no. control. Uuder the British North America Act such matters are relegated to the Provincial Legislatures, and if there is any argument in favour of women being accorded the right to vote on account of their disability to exercise their influence with regard to these subjects, then the right to vote should be limited to the Provincial Legislatures, and not extended to the Dominion Parliament.
Another argument used in favour of woman suffrage is that women would exercise a most beneficial effect upon all questions of social and moral reform. Well, vve have had questions pertaining to social and moral reform before this Parliament and before the Legislatures of the several provinces for many years. We have had temperance legislation promoted in the various provinces. We know that in three of the provinces at' least there is practically total prohibition. The women of this country are naturally interested in the question of temperance. It is to the highest degree commendable in them that they have always given their influence on
9 p.m. the side of temperance. But , they have made their influence felt in the legislation adopted by this Parliament and by the legislatures of the provinces on this subject. In Nova Scotia

we have practically total prohibition. In Saskatchewan they have prohibition to the extent that there is no such thing as a liquor business carried on by private individuals. And there are assurances that Alberta will have prohibition within the next few years. These reforms have been brought about notwithstanding that women have no votes and have not occupied seats in the provincial legislatures or in this Parliament. There is a stronger feeling in favour of Dominion-wide prohibition today, I believe, than ever before. On all sides we see evidence that the temperance movement has received enormous momentum within the last few years, and we have every reason to believe that there will be more temperance legislation within the next few years than in all the previous history of the Dominion. And all this is brought about by representatives in the . legislatures and in the Parliament of Canada among whom women do not sit. Mere men are willing to give ear to pleas for social and moral reform; and I question very much if the influence of women, if they were given the right to vote and to sit in Parliament, would be more potent than it is at the present time. Has there ever come up in this Parliament a question in which the rights and interests of women have been discriminated against as compared with men? Very few subjects are dealt with in this Parliament in which * women have an exclusive interest? Take our criminal law, as an example. There is not a line from one end to the other of that code that discriminates against women. On the contrary, exceptions are made in favour of women under the provisions of the criminal law that do not apply to men. Therefore, women cannot ask the right to vote on the ground that because they do not exercise the franchise theiir interests are not safeguarded in Parliament or in the legislatures of this country.
Women's condition in the scheme of citizenship has been vastly improved by the legislation of the last hundred years. The Married Women's Property Act, which has been placed upon the statute-books of the various provinces of this Dominion within comparatively recent years, accords to women the right to exercise control over their own property which they did not exercise fifty ot a hundred years ago. It was brought to the attention of the representatives of the people in the legislatures of Canada that the right of property was not enjoyed by married women to the same extent as by men, and immediately these
legislatures took up this question and enacted laws on the subject of women's property, so that to-day women exercise practically the same control over their property as men do with respect to the property which they own.	.
Woman suffrage is demanded because it is complained that virtuous and intelligent women have no votes, while male illiterates and drunkards have the right to vote. I ask, are all women virtuous and temperate? I am willing to concede that the exceptions are not so numerous among women.as among men; nevertheless, if you are going to extend the franchise to women you will be extending it to some who are of the same class as those among men whose exercise of the rlight to vote is objected to. We have in some provinces a limited franchise. In the province of Nova Scotia, and I think in New Brunswick and Ontario, and some other provinces as well, there is a property franchise upon which the right to vote is based. In Nova Scotia, before a person is permitted to vote, he must show that he is the owner of real estate to the value of $1&0 at least or is in receipt of an income of $250 a year. But in the province of Manitoba, if I am correctly informed, there is manhood suffrage. Every male person of the age of 21 years has the right to have his name placed on the electoral list, quite irrespective of whether or not he owns property. The same law prevails in the province of Saskatchewan, and, I have no doubt, also in Alberta and possibly in British Columbia. Therefore you have an adult suffrage in these provinces. If the principle contended for by my hon. friend from St. John is carried, you not only place the women owning property upon the electoral list, but you put upon the electoral list the name of every woman 21 years of {ige whether she owns property or not. As I say, you take in the whole scope of the female population of these provinces, and again I ask are there no drunkards among the women of these provinces?
No.

I do not know; but I do
know that in some countries we sometimes find that the virtue of sobriety is not as universal among the women as we would like it to be.

That is not so in the
West though.

If such a thing happened
that there were any women in those prov-

inces where manhood suffrage is enjoyed who do not possess the highest standard of sobriety and morality, they would be equally objectionable as voters as those male electors of whom the women complain. You have these undesirables, if there be any, placed upon the electoral list, and I should like to know how much more the undesirable female voter would improve the moral condition of this country than the undesirable male voter. Government means force; it means endurance; it means physical power. Voters do not make Governments. The decrees of Governments are not enforced mechanically or automatically. After laws are passed in the legislatures and Parliaments it is necessary to give effect to them, very frequently by force. Our civic ordinances are enforced by certain officers who constitute the police force in the community where the ordinances apply. Our national laws are enforced very frequently by our soldiers and international rights are necessarily enforced by arms. If women claim that they occupy the same position exactly in the scheme of citizenship that men do, then how are their laws going to be enforced, because there will be no distinction? They say that in all respects they are equal to men and they are prepared to assume the same burdens that are imposed upon men. Then if that be true women must assume the garb of the police officer if she represents the public in civic matters. Her sisters, by virtue of whose support perhaps she occupies a seat in the civic or municipal council, must assume the garb of policemen and must do pelice duty to enforce civic laws. If rebellion breaks out in this country it is necessary to call out the militia. There is no reason why the militia force should be confined to the men, because if the resolution of the hon, member for St. John passes and women become as important a factor in the government of this country as men, then they must have the same obligations imposed upon them, and these women must be prepared to shoulder their guns, to march out and take their places in the trenches, and to do their full share in enforcing the laws which they are parties in the making. We have a condition of affairs existing now which shows how futile would he the assertion of international rights if they were not backed up by force of arms. Advocates of woman suffrage, if the ideal conditions are brought about which they have in mind, must agree that women shall constitute part of our armies and shall endure the same hardships, the same discomforts and the same 
privations that are endured by the men now occupying the trenches. It is folly to say that women are physically the equal of men. In some other respects they are superior to men.
Those in favour of women having the right to vote seem to be influenced by two notions. One is resentment at the suggestion that women should be counted by men as inherently inferior in certain respects. The second is reprehension of a state of society in which more money, * more personal liberty, more power, more public recognition and happier psychological conditions fall to the share of men. The interference in polities on the part of woman I very much fear is more likely to degrade women than her influence is calculated to .elevate politics. We do know that in certain states of the Union women have enjoyed the right to vote, for 48 or 50 years. Twelve states have adopted prohibition with men alone voting, while only four states have adopted prohibition with the aid of women's votes. The State of Maine, which has defeated every attempt to introduce woman suffrage, has had prohibition since 1850. NoTth Dakota, which defeated woman suffrage at the polls in 1914, has had prohibition since 1889. Not a single state went dry with women voting before Nov. 3, 1914. According to Senator Works of California, the city of San Francisco has 3,500 saloons. The male suffrage city of Boston, with a population one and one-half times as large as San Francisco, has only about 700 saloons. On May-4, 1915, the women of Reno, exercising the franchise for the first time, voted against the proposition to reduce the numbeT of saloons from 80 to 40, and were publicly thanked by the liquor interests for standing by them. After 46 years of woman suffrage, the State of Wyoming is still wet. Colorado, woman suffrage since 1893, adopted prohibition Nov. 3, 1914, but the city of Denver, under the local option provision for cities of 50,000 and over, voted to remain wet.
I cite these facts for the purpose of showing that one of the reasons advanced in favour of woman suffrage has not been realized as respects prohibition. Originally, when this agitation was let loose' in the United States, the contention was made that woman had the inalienable right to exercise the franchise and have her name placed on the electoral list. The Supreme Court of the United States, 20 years ago, upon that matter being referred to them, declared unanimously that women had no

inalienable right whatever in regard to the matter. So the advocates of woman suffrage were obliged to shift their ground and they based their argument on the claim that, while they did not have a right to claim the exercise of. the franchise, it was desirable in the public interest because their influence would be so elevating on all subjects of social and moral reform. The facts I have cited as to the influence of women voters on the prohibition question in the portions of the United States where they exercise the franchise, goe^ to show that no marked advancement has been brought about by reason of their exercising that privilege. As I stated a moment ago, the granting to women of the right to vote does not settle anything whatever. In .the province of Manitoba the legislators recognized) that fact; they felt it would be useless and futile to stop at giving women the mere right to vote, so they coupled with it the necessary corollary of giving them the right to sit in Parliament. I repeat, there is no question as to women being inferior or unequal to men in any way, but there is a vast difference between the functions of women as compared with those of men. In every well-regulated family the work is divided among its members, so that each duty is assigned to such member as should most properly perform. Take a homely illustration from country life. The father and sons do the outside work, while the household duties are performed by the mother and daughters. Now, any rearrangement of those duties, that would place the mother and daughters upon the roof of the barn to repair the leak, and the father and sons in charge of the pastry and needlework, would be universally regarded as highly inequitable and improper. Votes for women mean foT the suffragette not only the right to vote, but the right to canvass in elections, to serve upon committees, to attend caucuses, to sit in Parliament, to have no time left to devote to those tender duties for which she alone in . the whole creation is specially fitted. The division of labour that I referred to a moment ago was decreed by God himself and honoured and respected by man throughout all the ages. It implies no lack of capacity, no inferiority, on the part of women. It is the sturdy trees of the forest that beaT the brunt of the storms, and thus afford shelter to the tender foliage that vegetates beneath their protecting branches.
The agitation for women suffrage began in the United States some seventy years
ago, and it has been going on merrily ever since. It is quite true that in some of the Western States they have succeeded in getting the suffrage as respects State elections, but during those seventy years every attempt made to grant women the right to vote in federal elections has been persistently and consistently opposed. I recognize and appreciate the character and quality of the citizens of the United States, and there	are many	respects inwhich they can set us an example, in certain	departments	of government, as well as regards intellectual development; but there are other aspects of their social and civic life from which I would not like to borrow, or which I would care to have engrafted upon the body politic of this country. There are two evils from which the United States has suffered as no other country in the world has suffered; the first is that of divorce, and the other arises from the agitation lor woman's suffrage. I submit Mr. Speaker that the agitation for woman suffrage bids fair to rob the people of the United States of the remnant of domestic and social life which has been left to them by their divorce laws. The agitators in favour of woman suffrage would call her away from the functions which she was designed by nature to perform, and would change her from the gentle creature that we have always known her to be into a raving militant suffragette. The agitation in England has been such as to leave a blot upon the civilization of that country. Advocates of woman suffrage say that the women would eAnoble public life. I would ask if they approve of the actions of the militant suffragettes in England previous to the war. There was no breach of the peace, no destruction of property, no invasion of private rights which they failed to conceive and carry out. The jails were filled, week in and week out, with the women who believed that by those methods, and those methods alone, they -would be able to carry out the reform which they sought to establish.
I referred a moment ago to the consequences upon the social life of the United States of the advocacy of woman suffrage. I will quote a few statistics shoeing the result of the agitation during recent years.
In the House of Representatives, January 12, the proposed suffrage amendment to the Federal Constitution was defeated by a vote of 174 yeas to 204 nays, with 57 representatives not recorded. In a full House the suffragists would have needed 290 votes to carry the amendment. They fell 116

short of that. On the vote recorded they needed 252 votes. They fell 78 short of that.
The following were the results so far as the 'legislatures are concerned. In Alabama, the suffrage amendment for which the suffragists had made an active campaign, did not get out of committee. In Arkansas, the suffrage amendment was crowded out by the provision that only three constitutional amendments can be submitted at dne time. In Connecticut, the proposed amendment was defeated in the House by a vote of 106 yeas to 124 nays. In Delaware, the proposed amendment was defeated in the House by a vote Of 8 yeas to 22 nays, and in the Senate by 6 yeas to 11 nays. In Florida, the proposed suffrage amendment was defeated. In Georgia, a resolution for the submission of a suffrage amendment was laid on the table by a unanimous vote by the Legislative Committee. In Illinois, the resolution for a constitutional convention, for which the suffragists laboured, in the expectation that the convention, if it met, would make full suffrage one of its chief considerations, failed to pass the House after receiving a nearly unanimous vote in the Senate. In Indiana, a limited suffrage Bill, after the Illinois model, was defeated. In Maine, the proposed suffrage amendment was defeated in the House. In Michigan, the suffrage attempt to secure the enactment of a limited suffrage Bill failed because .the Bill was found to. be unconstitutional. In Minnesota, the proposed suffrage amendment was defeated in the Senate. In Missouri, the attempt to persuade the- legislature to resilbmit the suffrage amendment which was defeated at the polls last year by a majority of 140,206 failed. In Nebraska, a limited suffrage Bill was defeated. In New Hampshire, a municipal suffrage Bill was defeated in the House by a vote of 121 yeas to 230 nays, an adverse majority of nearly two to one. In North Carolina, a proposed suffrage amendment was indefinitely postponed by the House by a vote of 68 to 39. In North Dakota, the proposed suffrage amendment, which passed the 1913 legislature, came up for the required action by a second legislature, but was tabled in the Senate by a vote of 26 to 21. In Oklahoma, the proposed suffrage amendment was indefinitely postponed in the Senate. In Rhode Island, a presidential suffrage Bill was defeated in the House by a vote of 65 to 31. In Vermont, a combined presidential and municipal suffrage Bill was defeated in the House by a vote of 129 to 100. 
In Wisconsin, the resolution providing for the submission of a suffrage amendment to the electors was defeated in the House, April 20, and in the Senate, July 1.
The results at the polls were: In New Jersey, October 19, for the suffrage amendment, 1133,201; against, 184,474; majority against, 51,273. In Massachusetts, November 2, for the suffrage amendment, 162,482; against, 295,939; majority against, 133,487. In New York, November 2, for the suffrage amendment, 544,457; against, 732,770; majority against, 188,313. Unofficial anti-suffrage majority in Oneida county, 6,154, making the total majority against, 194,467. In Pennsylvania, November 2, for the suffrage amendment, 385,348; against, 441,034; majority against, 55,686.
If after seventy, years of agitation in the United States these important and wealthy states of the Union have pronounced so decisively against female suffrage, how can my hon. friend from St. John hope that this Parliament is going to accept his resolution upon a mere moment's notice? He stated in his opening remarks with much pride that thirty years ago he had proposed a similar resolution in the legislature of New Brunswick. I commend him for his persistency, I commend him for the consistency of his course, but inasmuch as the legislature of New Brunswick has not yet accepted female suffrage, the hon. gentleman cannot boast of the success that has crowned his efforts.
I am opposed to the resolution of the hon. member for St. John because it imposes an obligation upon the vast majority of the women of this country that they are unwilling to assume. The right to vote is not a contest between the women in the United States and England who seek the franchise and the men who are opposed to it. I say, and I say with authority, that the contest, both in England and the United States, is rather between the women who are in favour of the exercise of the suffrage and the vast majority of the women in those countries who do not want to exercise the suffrage. Take a poll of the women in England, and a poll of the women in the different states of the Union in which this agitation is going on, and it will be found that there is a vast majority of women who are opposed to woman suffrage. So far as this country is concerned,
I am unwilling that this Parliament shall impose upon the vast majority of women an obligation which they are unwilling to asume, which they do not wish to assume and which, according to all womanly and motherly instincts, they ought not to be

asked to assume. If the resolution of the hon. member for St. John becomes crystallized into law we will bequeath to our children, and our children's children, a social and domestic life as bald and barren as the mountains of Gilboa.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the wide difference of opinion which exists between such weighty men as the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs ley, and the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), and in order that they may have an opportunity, between now and a future session, of adjusting their differences amicably, and as there is a great number of gentlemen on this side of the House who desire to speak on this most important subject on a future occasion, I move the adjournment of the debate.
No, no.
It is moved by Mr. Bennett that the debate be now adjourned.

I think that upon reflection my hon. friend'(Mr. Bennett) will see that .it is hot desirable to press this motion. It is quite early in the evening and my motion has stood over on quite a number of occasions when it was called particularly at the request of members of the Government. It having now come up for consideration I think it is desirable, if possible, to take a vote upon it to ascertain what is the opinion of the House .so that the Government may be guided by that opinion. If the House should be in favour of refusing the motion, of course, the Government will act accordingly. If the House should be of the opinion that the motion should carry, I think it is desirable that it should be so informed at as early a time as possible, because Manitoba has passed woman suffrage. There are two vacancies in Manitoba, and unless the legislation is made clear there will be inextricable confusion in connection with these elections when they come on. There will be many lawyers, I venture to say, who will claim that women have the right to vote for members of Parliament. There will be many others who will say that they have not the right to vote. It is desirable to make it clear. If the motion stands over to-night by the ingenuity of my hon. friend, it may not come up again during the present 'session, as the 'Government have given notice that they are going to take Wednesdays, and Government business will have precedence on that day. I would therefore ask my hon. friend not to press this motion.
Mr. ROGERS. In answer to my hon. friend, I may say that this is undoubtedly a very important question that has been raised, and, in so far .as any fear my hon. friend may have with respect to the question not again being brought to the attention of the House, I assure him that the question will come up again before the close of the session. It is an important question and we are most desirous of disposing of it in the most reasonable and the clearest manner possible. Therefore, I entirely agree with my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) in moving the adjournment of the debate.
Mr. GEORGE E. McCRANEY (Saskatoon) :	Mr. Speaker, before the motion to
adjourn the debate is put, I would like to say a few words as coming from the province of Saskatchewan, which is one of the provinces that in the very near future will adopt suffrage for women,
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion of the hon. member for East Simcoe?
Carried.
No.

lost.

As has been pointed
out in the House already, the province of Manitoba has passed a resolution which will give the franchise to the women of that province. The legislature of the province of Saskatchewan is now in session and Mr. Walter Scott has given the assurance that similar legislation will be passed. In Manitoba a very large petition was presented by the women of the province asking for the franchise. The same has been done in Saskatchewan-	,

I am afraid my hon.
friend is rather out of order in view of the fact that the debate has been adjourned.
