The hon. member for
East Simcoe made a motion to adjourn the debate and I declared the motion lost.

I do not know whether or not a petition was presented to the legislature of Alberta, but that legislature is now in session, and the Premier of the province has pledged that there also

woman suffrage will be granted. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Kyte) argued that if these women were given the franchise they would have to assume obligations different from those assumed by men in respect of the franchise-as though they had not the right to exercise the franchise as men do. If women are given the franchise, those who do not care to exercise it may stay at home, as the men do when they do not wish to exercise it. The motion of the hon. member for St. John city does not seek to impose woman suffrage upon the county of Richmond; it simply asks that any province desiring to do so may have the right to give their women a voice in public affairs. This has no reference to the question of prohibition. In the province of Manitoba, women will not vote in the plebiscite which is to be taken on the thirteenth of next month. Women had no part in the vote which was taken last summer in the province of Alberta. In Saskatchewan it had already been determined to take a vote on the question of prohibition, and it is only because that vote has been accelerated that in the meantime women will be given the right to vote.
But what is the real reason why we should give women votes if they want them? We have learned many things from the war, and one thing that I believe we have learned more than any other is that women are able to take a place in public affairs that we had not previously thought them capable of. Their patriotic instincts have been a surprise to us; they have shown an ability to organize and a desire to advance national welfare which entitled them-at least in our province, we think-to take part in public affairs. In no province has the right of women been more fully recognized than in my own province-in the. matter of their being given a right similar to dower, in the matter of their rights in cases of intestacy, in the matter of their right to vote in municipal and school elections. The right which I have last mentioned is extended to unmarried as well as to married women. There are reasons why the western provinces recognize the copartnership of husband and wife in public affairs which may not apply with equal force in the eastern provinces. It is well known that in every new country the burden of settlement and of building up the community is borne by women as well as by men, indeed, as one who has lived quite a number of years in the West, I would say that those burdens fall more heavily upon the women than upon the men. The men of our
[Mr. McCraney.J
province and of the other Prairie Provinces wish to give women a share in public affairs because they recognize what women have done in the building up of the country.
My hon. friend has argued that if women take part in public life they will have to bear arms and act as the policemen of the country. That is as we will. If we say to the women: you must bear arms and be policemen, I am quite sure that there are many of them who will do so and will do it well. In any such argument there is no appeal to our chivalry, and I am quite sure that my hon. friend was not in serious vein when he made use of it. The fate of this motion has been indicated; it will probably arrive at nothing more than discussion this session. But I believe that after women shall have been given an opportunity to take part in the public affairs and have shown their capacity to do so, we shall have in all our legislatures a >
better class of men than we have had hitherto. That result in itself would be sufficient. In view of the results which have come from the part taken by women in elections, I do not think this Parliament should refuse to give to the women of the western provinces who already have a vote in municipa' affairs the right to exercise the franchise as proposed by the hon. member for St. John city.

I regret to
have to differ from the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) in that I think the franchise should be extended only to widows and spinsters.
You think they are the most sensible.

No, but a widow may toe the head of a family, and may take great interest in the affairs of her country. In Ontario the right to vote in municipal elections has been extended to widows and spinsters who hold property, and it was recently proposed to extend this right to provincial elections. If the resolution of the hon. member were limited to widows, and spinsters, I should feel disposed to support it, but I do not feel disposed to support a proposal to extend the franchise to married women, thus introducing into the home matters of political discussion and dissension.
You are a man of peace.

The home is sacred and no cause for dissension or quarrelling should be introduced into it. Often per-

sons who marry entertain opposite political views and controversy may arise, but in the case of widows and spinsters there would be no danger of that. Parliament and the provincial legislatures may enact laws affecting the property and civil rights of women, and I think they should have the right to exercise the franchise. At one time the franchise was limited to a certain class of persons who had to own property assessed for a certain amount; but when this Parliament accepted the provincial franchise in 1898, that was done away with. In Ontario the provincial franchise is very wide, including every British subject of twenty-one years of age. Now, as men 'in all countries have always held a higher place than women, the privileges can still be given to men and not extended to women. There may be some agitation in some of the provinces for female suffrage, but I do not know that it is very wide in the province' of Ontario, and I have never heard of any agitation in my county. I, one time, was at a meeting of the Ontario Liberal Association and a lady who was supposed to be the president of the Women's Suffrage Association at Toronto wanted to have the privilege of addressing the meeting. We gave her that privilege and, after she had addressed us, I asked her whether, if we adopted her programme, she would work for the Liberal party. Well, she told us that women should not have any party. Now, if the, women have not decided what party they belong to, or if they do not belong to any party, I do not think it will be of much use to grant them the franchise. Some years ago I read a speech delivered by Mr. Justice Longley, of Nova Scotia, in which he admitted the great influence that women exercised over the affairs of our country. We all know from history that women have always played great parts in the ruling of various countries; we have all read of the great ladies of France 'and England; we have heard of petticoat governments; that is, of governments ruled by the influence of women, but Mr. Justice Longley said that he had never seen a woman very anxious for the * franchise unless she had lost all confidence in her charms. I believe that, although women are denied the right to cast their vote, many men deposit their ballots according to the will of their wives, and that women, if they so desire, can exert a great	influence in the
election of members of this House as well as of members of the different
provincial legislatures. I do not want to detain the House any longer, but if this resolution comes to a vote, I am afraid I shall have to record my vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that -I was not in the House when my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) proposed his motion, but I have gathered that his proposition is one that would lead to the gradual substitution of the vivacity of women in the affairs of the state for what is usually the crass stupidity of men, the quickness of observation of the female sex for what is the absolute dullness of man, and, if I have rightly gathered the object and purport of the motion, then I now hold with my hon. friend from St. John. I support the motion on very broad grounds. It seems to me that, for the ordinary purposes of the nation, the duties of men and women are pretty equally divided, and it would not be regular nor proper, nor even possible to endeavour to carry on the general purposes of the nation without women. Every one must realize, if he will reflect for a moment, that he had a woman for his mother, and, if he happens to have a daughter, she is a woman also, and he cannot get married without having a woman to help him to the business. The two sexes are really absolutely necessary for carrying on human affairs. A proper appreciation of this elementary fact on the part of my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) would have kept him from delivering what I think was the weakest logic and one of the weakest speeches to which I have ever listened. I have frequently listened to my hon. friend and he always delivers an eloquent speech, and sometimes a comprehensive and logical one, so that I am inclined to be charitable enough to attribute the weakness of his logic in this case to the feebleness of his subject, or to the absolute want of any subject at all.
The greatest political evil that we have in Canada at the present moment is political corruption. I am sure I am right in this, because if I did not know it was so, I was told so by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) the other day. I have asked a good many very observant and very knowing people of both sexes what they thought would be woman's attitude towards political corruption. Nine out of ten observers, whose opinion I would value, at once answered: " Oh, you cannot buy an average woman at all to do anything against her will," and

that is just my opinion of the sex, having seen a great deal of them in all the avefiues of life that are followed by medical men. Therefore I think that the greatest political evil existing m this country at the present time would almost cease to exist if you had many women taking interest in politics as men do to-day. But perhaps one can best demonstrate the strength of the position of my hon. friend from St. John by looking at a few of the arguments advanced by my hon. friend from Richmond. My hon. friend said, in referring to an argument which I have always thought a very small one, as to a certain number of women being intemperate, that, after all, in enfranchising women we should enfranchise such women, and therefore the case would not be mended as against the fact that there are a certain number of intemperate men at the present time. He said-and I think in saying it he gave away his case-that in enfranchising women we should be dealing with the same class as men belong to, although I admit that he modified his opinion.
I have already said that the strongest argument for woman suffrage is the fact that women do belong to the same great human family that men do. If my hon. friend had extended his observation a little further he would have seen that the restricted application of his argument was wrong, and that the wider application of it absolutely takes the ground from under his own case.
The hon. gentleman said that if woman suffrage were granted we should need to make women policemen. As my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) has said, that would not necessarily follow. But 1 agree with my hon.' friend from Saskatoon .that if we do make women policemen they would be very efficient ones. I never saw a man so far gone in crime, so very much the worse for liquor, that he would not rather be taken to a cell by a woman than by a man. In fact, the great majority of criminals, unless the most desperate class among them, would accept the gentle leadership of women and make the duties of policemen very much easier than sometimes they are at present.
Then the hon. gentleman said that we should have to be prepared to put women in khaki and send them to the trenches. Why, he misses the whole case that women set up for the vote, the whole case that reformers put up for woman suffrage. Is there a member of this House who does not know that if woman had the vote there [Mr. M. Clark. 1
would be no trenches and no khaki, in a very short time? They would put an end to war, they would not be such fools as men are; they would take the more rational, elevated path of reason for the settlement of international disputes. Such, at any rate, is the argument of the social reformer. It does not meet the case to say that we1 should have to dress women in khaki and send them to the trenches after khaki and the trenches had been done away with.
Then my hon. friend had a very eloquent passage about the weakness of woman and the strength of man. There is perhaps no one who can so fully understand the erroneous nature of that argument as a medical man. I recall a story that Max O'Rell used to relate, and which I think he has put in one of his books. He tells of listening to a bunch of men talking about a woman acquaintance of theirs who had to undergo an operation without chloroform, and one of them spoke of her admiringly as having " stood it like a man." There is not a woman who does not 10 p.m. know, and there are not many men who do not know, that if she had only stood it like a man she would not have stood it at all like a woman. I have seen many a man go into fits of fear and desperation about an ailment that a woman, if he had consulted her, could have told hinj meant that there was nothing particular the matter with him. Take it from me, Sir-and in this I speak more dogmatically than I usually speak-that for endurance, for patience, for all the virtues of that kind, no man.who knows himself and also knows woman will ever put himself in comparison with a woman for a moment. 'That is my experience; I give it for what it is worth. And I do not think that any man in this House really disagrees with me.
My hon. friend admitted that in a great many ways which he did not mention women are the superiors of men. That scarcely seems an argument for the inferiors keeping their superiors out of the vote. I submit for his consideration that that admission of his wrecked another portion of his platform beneath his feet.
The hon. gentleman seemed to argue that women, if given the vote, would vote against prohibition. Well, there is something to be said on both sides of the prohibition question. I am not now discussing the question of prohibition in its restricted sense as applied to the sale of liquor; but on general principles I am very much in favour of freedom, as this House well knows. It is freedom we are fighting for in Europe,

and it is freedom for which men have been willing to lay down their Jives throughout all ages of the world's history. So, if a woman has an instinctive or intuitive prejudice against prohibition, even of intoxicating liquors, she has, I say, the mental characteristic possessed by the best men throughout the ages of human history. She possibly has some little sex and domestic reason for being opposed to prohibition-if she be opposed to it, as the hon. gentleman suggests; and I only meet the statement as he makes it. Nothing would terrify a married woman more than the thought that she had to have her bus-band, dangling on her hands, morning, noon and night. Nothing bothers a woman's life more than to have a man of that kind. There are exceptions, of course, but the exceptions only prove the rule. The woman, like the man, likes to have a little time to herself, and it may be a little domestic prejudice that gives her that view of prohibition, if my hon. friend is right, and she really does hold that view.
My hon. friend said he would not like to have the women of Canada turned into the militant suffragettes of Britain. Well, I rather admire the militant suffragettes of Britain from this point of view, that I recollect what men had to do in Britain before they got the vote. I know something about the Chartist movement. I have heard of the massacre of Peterloo, and the riots that men had to betake themselves to before they got the vote. And, after all is said and done, if the women in Great Britain are so determined to have the vote that they have proceeded to certain practices which to the men now comfortably ensconced in their privilege seems reprehensible, I would remind the hon. gentleman and those who think with him that women are only paying to men the sincerest form of flattery by imitating them in this respect, and that they are being met only as entrenched privilege has always met the demands of the people for enfranchisement and the broadening of their rights.
In this connection, the hon. gentleman used an expression which to my mind was distinctly alarming. If he could prove his case, I am sure he would change my position on this subject, and I think he would change the position not only of all the men but of all the women in Canada who think with me on this question. He said that the women would become " bearded Amazons." If he means that literally, and had said only "Amazons," I would not have been so alarmed, but when he spoke of them becoming
"bearded Amazons" he seemed to think that ten'e of the results of the extension of the suffrage would be that they would at once proceed to grow beards. If this part of his case could be proven I believe it would change the attitude of every supporter, male or female, on my side of the case. But I do not think that his physiological knowledge would enable him to place the proof in such a shape before us that we should be convinced that he has the correct view of this matter. In the same connection he said that it would interfere with the performance of the functions proper to women. I think that in that he held out a more alarming prospect even than that of the growth of beards on the part of women-that the extension of the suffrage to women would lead to the extinction of the species. I desire to reassure him, when that state of affairs comes about we shall be so near to the millennium that all these questions of suffrage, and prohibition, and the others that occupy our minds will have ceased to interest us. But I think that for the present he need not be alarmed, over any such prospects as either the general growth of beards by women or the extinction of the species.
The weakest argument that the hon. gentleman used he used last. He said that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was presenting a professed reform which bad been rejected in that enlightened country, the United States, for seventy years. My answer to him upon that point would be: Just think of the weakness of any reformer-though I am sure you will never find it in the hon. member for St. John city-who would cease to attack any evil simply because it has been supported for seventy years. If the argument meant anything, it meant that if a political ^evil is old enough, it should not be interfered with. There is nothing in the way of reform that has not been fought for, not merely for seventy years but for centuries. Why, parliamentary institutions had existed in Britain for hundreds of years before the first Reform Bill, which was passed, as you remember, Mr. Speaker, in 1832. By that Reform Bill, as an elementary knowledge of English history reminds us, boroughs were destroyed where there were only two houses and, in other cases, where were not more than five voters. That -state of affairs had existed for the hundreds of years that Britain had parliamentary institutions before the destruction of the rotten boroughs. Would it have been logical, while Macaulay was de-

livering his wonderful speech on the Reform Bill, or when Grey was laying the foundations of the first extension of political liberty in Britain; would it have been logical to go before the British House of Commons and say: You must not attack this evil of restricted franchise; it has existed for centuries? I think my hon. friend will say that that would have been a most illogical position. Reformers have never taken that attitude. For a period of thirty-five years after the first Reform Bill was passed, from 1832 to 1867, the reformers worked for househld suffrage in the boroughs of England. In 1867 they got it, from a Tory Government. From 1867 to 1885, a period of nearly twenty years, the workmen in the boroughs had the vote, but the workmen in the counties did not have it. The reformers went on working for the next twenty years, and then the workmen in the counties got it. That was thirty years ago, Mr. Speaker, and they have not manhood suffrage in Britain yet; but manhood suffrage will come by the same patient per-severaance against odds and difficulties and prejudices by which the other extensions of the suffrage came. Woman suffrage may be right or it may be wrong, but it is neither right nor wrong because the United States has refused it for the last seventy years.
From a careful study of the qualities of the sexes, I am persuaded that women have more endurance than men, tnat they see more quickly, that they see further than men, that their moral qualities along other lines are higher than those of men. I am persuaded that vfhen they get an equal voice in public affairs, as they always take very good care to have more than an equal voice-and with our consent-in domestic affairs, I am persuaded that it will be a better world to live in, and that the countries that adopt this reform will be better countries to live in. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the motion of the hon. member for St. John City.

I think that some irregularity might result from giving the franchise to women, in provinces where they already have the right to vote in provincial elections. Throughout the Dominion we. have pretty much the same kind of voting in all the provinces; it is nearly all based upon the principle of manhood suffrage. This condition results .in the vote being equalized throughout the Dominion! if this resolution should become law, however, some inequalities would exist.
I am - not one of those who had to wait for the war, as the hon. member for Saskatchewan evidently did, to find out that women are equal to men in business as well as in other respects. My experience is that, so far as business is concerned, women are quite equal to men. I would just as lief have women on a board of directors as men. I am not making any reflection on the ability of the men, but I am in dead earnest when I say that, so far as my experience goes in business matters, women have just as much ability as men have.
As to their other qualities, we all know them. Women are the salvation of humanity. Were it not for the influence for good that women exert over men, we would be a fine bunch. As to the argument that the granting of the vote would change them, I doubt that. As a matter of fact, women are a powe"r behind the Throne, and they exert a great deal of influence on elections, as we all know. There are few men who are not influenced more or less for good by women. The finer instincts of men are due, I think, to the influence of their mothers, and when a man grows up be derives the best kind of influence from the women who surround him. If a man has a mother and sisters, even when he comes to my age, their influence over him is certainly good. Therefore, I think their influence upon politics would be equally good. In all probability this resolution will not go much further to-night, but I see a difficulty in this that the women in one province would have votes while those in another province would have no votes. That does not seem to me to be putting them on an equality. As for the argument that if we give women the right to vote, we must give them the 76
right to sit in Parliament, I can only say that that would be no hazard for me. I would be very glad to welcome my sisters in Parliament if they wished to sit here and were elected. I assure you they would elevate the tone of Parliament. Outside of the question of inequality in the franchise throughout the different provinces, I am certainly in favour of giving women the franchise, but I would not like to force it upon any woman who does not want it. I do not agree that women should he given the right to vote even if they did not exercise it. It is one of the drawbacks of our electoral system, that a great many men do not vote. That is one of the reasons why there is so much corruption in elections; they do not vote, or they vote during the last hour. I do not believe in passing laws that will not be lived up to, and I do not agree with my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney). If the women of this country demand the right to vote, by all means give it to them, they are perfectly capable of exercising it but if they do noi want to vote, and they will not vote, then by no means give it to them.

Might I ask my hon.
friend if in connection with the difficulty that is in his mind as to equalizing the vote in the different provinces he has kept in view the fact that each province has a fixed representation in this Parliament dependent on its entire population?

It might not alter the
representation of the provinces, but my hon. friend can easily see what I mean, that in one province the women would have the right to vote, while in another province only the men would have the vote, so that they would have a double franchise in one province, and only a single franchise in another.

They would have the
same representation.
Suppose we went further and gave them representation according to the votes.

The British North
America Act assures that.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this question is one of sufficient importance to entitle us to expect that some hon. gentlemen on the Government side of the House will indicate the attitude of the Government with regard to it. The matter has not been br'ought



forward as a party question in any sense, and the discussion has extended over a very wide range. The proposition submitted in the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Pugs-ley) does not necessarily involve a discussion of the wider question; it merely raises the point as to whether or not this Parliament should recognize a change in the franchise as might be brought about in the different provinces of the Dominion, in the direction of permitting women to vote. The views of hon. gentlemen who have spoken have varied as to the wisdom of such a change, and the discussion has been entirely apart from any political differences that exist in the House. As my hon. friend from St. John pointed out, the change is only imminent. Already, in one of the provinces, the franchise has been made sufficiently broad to permit the women to vote, and two other provinces are on the point of granting the same privilege. These provinces are in the West, and it has been urged by some hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-night that the conditions in those provinces are peculiar, that they are such that it is only natural and proper that the women should have the franchise. The question is whether or not we in this Parliament should recognize the View which has been adopted by those provinces in regard to this question, and I think the proposition is sufficiently important to justify some pronouncement on the part of the Government as to their attitude.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) has suggested that some reference should be made on this side of the House as to the attitude which the Government takes [DOT]in respect to the question under discussion. If I could believe that my hon. friend Who moved the resolution was quite sincere in presenting it to this House, I would be disposed to discuss it from a somewhat different viewpoint.
The hon. gentleman started out by telling the House that it was his privilege thirty years ago, when seeking election in a constituency in New Brunswick, to advance this same proposal of votes for women. But, strange to say, although my hon. friend from St. John has had ample opportunity, in his native province, from that time on, to secure the enactment of such legislation as would give the women of that province the right to exercise their franchise, which he is proposing here this evening for another province, he has not availed himself of that privilege. My hon. friend from Pictou has

apparently a doubt also whether this legislation should be extended to one particular province and not to all the provinces of Canada. When I suggested to my hon. friend from St. John that we amend his motion so as to provide for the extension of the privilege to the women in all the provinces of Canada he was not disposed to acquiesce in that proposal. I submit that if my hon. friend was sincere in the proposal which he has made he would have adopted this suggestion and then this House would have had something before it to consider in a tangible manner, and something that we would have reason to give very *serious (Consideration to. It has 'been suggested that the proposed resolution should be confined simply to one particular province which has already adopted the principal of woman suffrage-the province of Manitoba-and ,that it might be extended to any other province- that might follow Manitoba is example later on. 'The question is whether this Parliament should adapt a principle of a limited character or whether it should go the full length and adopt the principle of extending woman suffrage to all the provinces of Canada as well as to the individual provinces that might adopt it.
I am sure we all agree with the principle of equal rights to all the provinces. My hon. friend who sat down a few moments ago raised that particular question. I think he was quite right in saying that if we are to have woman suffrage in any one parti-' cular province we should have it in all the provinces of Canada. If the hon. member for St. John would amend his motion I would he disposed for one to give it consideration and to support a resolution by this House to extend the franchise to women in all parts of Canada.

How would my hon. friend reconcile that with the statement which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) is reported to have made that this Parliament would not interfere with the provincial franchise, but that the question must be left to the provinces to deal with?

We would not at all be interfering with the provincial franchise. Each province has the right to make its own franchise. If we extend the franchise we shall be extending it to all parts of Canada alike. I do not see that we would in any way be interfering with the provincial franchise, because it would apply to all the

provinces of Canada. We have a right in this Parliament to grant that extension if [DOT] we so wish. It is true, in view, as has been stated here this evening, of the part that our ladies have taken in the recent war, that they are entitled, if for no other reason, to full consideration and to all the rights that it is possible to extend to them in the matter of their franchise. That would be, therefore, a very powerful reason why this question should receive serious consideration at 'the hands of the members of this House.
As far as the franchise in the province of Saskatchewan is concerned, I would like to say t-hait in the last local election certain women were allowed to exercise their franchise, although there was no law of the province to enable them to do so. However, they were allowed that right, and they did really in certain places cast their votes.
Mr. MeCRANEY: I would like the hon. gentleman to tell me what riding he is referring to. I have never heard of any such incident.
Neither have I.

I do not remember the
particular riding but I remember the fact that ladies voted in certain parts of the province. I have the evidence to substantiate that statement, and I shall be glad to supply my hon. friend with sworn declaraiom of a scrutineer and naming the ladies who voted in that particular province in the election of 1912.
Mr. MeCRANEY: I would ask the minister to lay the declarations on the Table if he will.	.

I shall be very glad to
do that, and I shall be very glad to present the House with that sample, of the elastic manner in which the franchise of Saskatchewan was exercised in the election of 1912. At the same time, in that province, before the election, they removed that portion of the Act which provided that it was necessary for a man to be a British subject in order to vote at the election. It is true that some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House told us that that had been rectified later on. It was rectified but not until after the election was over, and in the event that there would be a Dominion election, it would be necessary for a man to be a British subject before he would be entitled to exercise the franchise in that province. We have no guarantee that the
76}	.
same province will not change the Act before the next general election thus repeating that which was done before the last election. It is their privilege, of course, if they desire to carry out their election law in that manner.	t
I do not believe it would be in the interest of the women of Manitoba, to have the franchise unless it were extended to all the provinces, and if my hon. friend had, as I suggested, amended his resolution to that extent, I would have been disposed to have supported him. But, in view of the fact that he has not done this, I will have to record my vote against his resolution and I will ask the members on this side to do likewise.

Mr,
Speaker, I want to say a word in favour of the resolution of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I shall content myself with saying that I shall be in favour of the resolution and until reasons are shown to me why the ladies should not be free in this country as well as the men, I mean to support all similar resolutions. I can hardly agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). His contention is that only a half loaf is offered to the ladies and that because they are not offered a whole loaf he is going to refuse them the half loaf. That is poor logic and I hardly think it will satisfy the ladies of this Dominion. I have a feeling that our ladies in Canada are thoroughly satisfied with the manner in which the men carry on the affairs of the country, but there is a desire that they should enjoy the same freedom and liberty as the men do. I therefore support the resolution of the hon. member for St. John.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), I believe, has alluded to some answer to a delegation which he stated I had given a year or two ago. Am I correct in that?
I do not think it was a year and a half ago-some months ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not received any delegation on the subject for a year and a half at least. I did in 1912, when in Great Britain, receive a delegation of ladies there; I think, in fact, there were two delegations, one supporting the idea that women should be invested with the franchise and the other opposing it. In the same year, 1912, I received. I believe, a delegation of ladies in Toronto, but I am not aware of having done so on any other

occasion. In regard to the delegation in Great Britain, I ventured, to say that I thought, in view of certain statements which were made, that the women of Canada were quite capable of looking after their own jnterests in such matters, and that the ladies of Great Britain would ijot require to interest themselves particularly in the matter in so far as this country was concerned.
My hon. friend refers, I understand, to the
answer I gave to that delegation. The answer I gave, as I recollect, was that, under the system which had prevailed in this country from 1897 or 1898, the Federal franchise had been made to depend on the franchises 'of the several provinces; that persons entitled to vote at provincial elections were entitled to vote at Federal elections; and I suggested to them that probably the ladies of Canada would find it desirable, in the first place, to address themselves to the provincial authorities. And I said, that until we departed from that system of having the franchise for Federal affairs dependent upon the franchises in the several provinces, such would be the proper course for them to take.
My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) has perhaps raised some considerations this evening which might make it desirable for us to take the whole question of the Federal franchise into consideration, and I do intend to take it into consideration in view of what the hon. gentleman has stated. When that question is so taken into consideration, the enfranchisement of women must be considered, not in relation to any individual province or provinces in Canada, but from the standpoint of the whole Dominion. We shall then be prepared to come to the House if necessary, with proposals based upon a wider conception of the matter than that which has impressed itself upon my hon. friend in proposing his motion. It would seem to be quite undesirable that we should be responsible for any enactment by which the women in one province of Canada should have the right to vote in Federal' elections, and the women in other provinces should not have that right. Upon reflection, hon. gentlemen must come to the conclusion that such a result, which is apparently desired by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) would not commend itself to the good sense of the members of the House, or to the good sense of the women of Canada. Therefore, it does not seem to me that the motion of the hon. gentleman,

which has in view the granting of the Federal franchise to women in some provinces of Canada and the withholding of it from women in other provinces, ought to commend itself to the good sense or the good judgment of the House. For my part, and reserving my right of judgment on the wider question, which is one of very great importance and which I shall be prepared to discuss at the proper time, I venture to submit that the proposal of the hon. gentleman ought not to command the support of hon. members, for the reason that, as regards the right to vote of one half the proposed electorate, it would create a discrimination in the franchise, as between the various provinces of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You are.

-and this must be a most remarkable question which I have presented to the attention of the Government; one so important that the Minister of Public Works wishes his party to vote it down, and
that my right hon. friend thinks it is going to- cause the repeal of the whole system under which the elections have been held for the past nineteen years, and that the Government must take up the responsibility and labour of evolving a new franchise Act for the purpose of carrying into effect the ideas which I venture to propound vthis evening in presenting this simple resolution, which might so easily and with such great, advantage be adopted by the House.
Now, just a word in answer to my hon. friend the member from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), who said that the only objection he had to the resolution was that it would prevent an equality in the electorate of the different provinces. That would not make any difference, as between the representation of the different provinces, because, under the British North America Act that representation is based entirely, upon population, and in any province, if there were ten times as many women as there are men, there would still ,be the same representation according to population. If ladies were allowed to vote in any one province, only between the people of that province would it make any difference, the number of representatives would remain the same; but a great deal might depend on the quality of the candidate who might be chosen by the people, because the women, if allowed to vote, might prefer one candidate to another, and they might succeed in electing a candidate who might not have been elected if men alone had the vote.
My right hon. friend says that there would be a difference in the franchise upon which the elections were held. That is the case to-day. In some provinces there is manhood suffrage, all men over twenty-one years of age having the right to vote if they have resided in a district for a very few months, whereas in other provinces no man has a right to vote unless he own3 four or five hundred dollars worth of real estate or personal property, or has an income to that amount.
What province is that?

I think the province of Prince Edward Island. The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) says that there is a property franchise in Nova Scotia. That must exclude many thousands in that province from voting.

manhood franchise.
I am told not.

I am told not; but suppose it were different, what is to hinder any province from going back to property franchise? What is to hinder any province from disfranchising thousands of men who in other provinces would be entitled to vote? Nothing at all. Therefore there is nothing in that argument. If this Parliament chooses to adopt the provincial franchise, to allow an election to take place on the provincial lists, I see no inconvenience and no difficulty whatever, in any province in which women are allowed to vote for members of the Provincial Legislature, being allowed the right to vote for members of Parliament. It must be borne in mind that this resolution merely- proposes:
That, in the opinion' of this House, it is desirable that the Government should promote legislation to amend the Dominion Elections Act, so as to provide that upon any province of Canada enacting legislation giving wcmen the right to vote for members of the Provincial Legislature, such women as are on the provincial voters' lists, or as are otherw'se entitled to vote for members of the legis'ature in such province, shall also, unless otherwise disqualified, have the right to vote at elec1 ions for members of this House.
If in the cours-e of time the other .provinces of Canada should follow the example of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, then women throughout Canada would be alloyed to vote; but so long as we act upon the provincial franchise and use the provincial lists, then with no degree of justice or fair play can we refuse to allow women whose names are on the provincial lists also to cast their vote for the members of the House of Commons. When I made my first observations in support of the resolution I did not think it necessary to present arguments- in favour of the general principle of giving women the right to vote; but if any such arguments were needed to support .such a -proposition such arguments were afforded by the speeches made by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), my hon. friend, from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) and my hon. friend from As-siniboia (Mr. Turriff). Their arguments were unanswerable, and to any fair-minded man they should fiave been convincing in favour of passing this resolution. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), and my Tight hon. friend the .Prime Minister need not pretend to the

women of this country that they are in favour of woman suffrage; they need not think for a single moment that they can keep thfs thing hanging before the women of this country for years and. make them believe that at some distant date, some time after the next election, in case the women should be foolish enough to give the Government their support, they will he willing to introduce a general franchise Act in which they will give women the right to vote.

That was your policy
thirty years ago.

To-day in the three Prairie Provinces, with a population of about 1,500,000, or one-fifth of the entire population of Canada, there is the opportunity of giving women tile right which they are demanding to-day, that is, to vote for members of this Parliament at the same time that they are given the right to vote for members of the legislatures of the three provinces.
Does the hon. member think that the women of Manitoba have any better right to vote than the women of New Brunswick?	- .

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege.

I desire to refer to the report of a recruiting meeting which I had the honour of addressing last night at Massey Hall in the city of Toronto. I find in this morning's Montreal Gazette a very fair and very complete report of that meeting, with one exception. There is one sentence in the report which gives it an altogether different meaning, and I deem it my duty to correct the mistaken impression at the earliest opportunity. In that report, I am made to say, in speaking of the bilingual question:
Why should they talk like that? Are there any difficulties to settle?
ThatAs far from what I said. The exact words are:
Why should there be difficulties to settle?
Which puts altogether a different meaning upon the whole report. The Toronto Globe, in a more lengthy report, after placing in my mouth the same question, gives my exact words. I followed up the statement. "Why should there be any difficulties to settle?" with the words:
I have met many people from all parts of the Dominion, and I am absolutely sure that there is not one man who is not perfectly willing that the French-Canadian jreop'e should be allowed to have their children learn French if they so des're, and to-night I tell you that there is not one French-Canadien who is not anxious to have his child or children taught to speak and understand the English language as I do.
The reports of La Patrie, the World and the Mail and Empire, as well as that , sent to other papers, by the Canadian Press Service are substantially correct. [DOT]
I did blame Bourassa and Lavergne in Toronto. I did not blame them for having been the cause of the bilingual trouble in Ottawa; I blamed Bourassa and Lavergne in Toronto as I would blame them in this House, and as I would blame them in any part of the province of Quebec, for having used the bilingual trouble in Ottawa or elsewhere in Ontario as an argument against recruiting in the province of Quebec. That is why I blamed them in Toronto, and that is why I will blame them at every pbssible opportunity in my own province. To-night I find in Le Devoir an article addressed to myself. It certainly dbes me too much honour. It is signed by one of the writers in Le Devoir, Mr. Omer Heroux. Before waiting even to see the Toronto papers, basing himself entirely upon the report of the meeting wired to the Gazette, he wrote a strong editorial concerning the statement attributed to me in Toronto last night. I am well aware of the difficulties in Ottawa. I am very sorry those difficulties should
exist; there is no reason why they should. I wish to correct the statement attributed to me; and I feel sure, knowing the honesty and integrity of Mr. Heroux, that he will correct the mistaken impression he has given respecting my statement. If he wishes to repeat exactly what I said, he will say that I blamed the editor of his paper, Mr. Bourassa and Mr. Armand Lavergne for using the bilingual question as an argument against recruiting in the good ol'd province of Quebec.
